c-us8-ov-gdp.text: In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series, in billions of chained 2017 dollars, real GDP was 7,257.3 in 1980, 8,537.0 in 1985, 10,055.1 in 1990, 11,413.0 in 1995, 14,096.0 in 2000, 15,988.0 in 2005, 16,349.1 in 2009, 16,789.8 in 2010, 18,799.6 in 2015, 20,715.7 in 2019, 20,284.5 in 2020, 23,394.9 in 2024 and 23,943.3 in 2025: about 3.3 times its 1980 level. It was lower in 2020 than in 2019.
c-us8-ov-gdp.label: approx
c-us8-ov-gdp.note: Chained-dollar levels change with each BEA revision. 'About 3.3 times' is this book's arithmetic (23,943.3 divided by 7,257.3).

c-us8-ov-pop.text: In BEA's series, in thousands, the population was 227,726 in 1980, 238,506 in 1985, 250,181 in 1990, 266,588 in 1995, 282,398 in 2000, 295,993 in 2005, 309,839 in 2010, 322,113 in 2015, 331,840 in 2020, 340,095 in 2024 and 341,944 in 2025: from about 228 million to about 342 million, a rise of about half.
c-us8-ov-pop.label: consensus

c-us8-ov-percap.text: Computed from BEA data, real GDP per person was about $31,900 in 1980 and about $70,000 in 2025, in chained 2017 dollars: about 2.2 times as much.
c-us8-ov-percap.label: approx
c-us8-ov-percap.note: This book's arithmetic: BEA's real GDP divided by BEA's population, rounded.

c-us8-ov-income.text: In the Census Bureau's series of real median household income, in what the series labels '2025 C-CPI-U Dollars', income was $61,910 in 1984, the series' first year; 63,090 in 1985, 67,050 in 1990, 66,990 in 1995, 73,560 in 2000, 72,810 in 2005, 74,810 in 2007, 71,790 in 2009, 70,110 in 2010, 69,070 in 2012, 74,590 in 2015, 85,320 in 2019, 83,590 in 2020, 81,460 in 2022, 85,210 in 2024 and 87,460 in 2025. It was about 41 percent higher in 2025 than in 1984, and it fell after 2007 and again after 2019.
c-us8-ov-income.label: approx
c-us8-ov-income.note: The series begins in 1984 and is expressed in C-CPI-U dollars; its levels depend on the price index used. The percentage is this book's arithmetic.

c-us8-ov-debt.text: In the Office of Management and Budget's series, by fiscal year, federal debt held by the public was 24.9 percent of GDP in 1980, 34.7 in 1985, 40.4 in 1990, 47.2 in 1995, 33.3 in 2000, 31.4 in 2001, 35.2 in 2005, 34.8 in 2007, 52.1 in 2009, 59.9 in 2010, 71.7 in 2015, 78.0 in 2019, 98.3 in 2020, 96.0 in 2024 and 97.8 in 2025.
c-us8-ov-debt.label: consensus

c-us8-reagan-1980.text: In the 1980 election Ronald Reagan won 489 electoral votes and 50.7 percent of the popular vote; Jimmy Carter won 49 electoral votes and 41.0 percent, and John Anderson, an independent, 6.6 percent.
c-us8-reagan-1980.label: consensus

c-us8-reagan-rates.text: The top federal income-tax rate was 70 percent in 1981, 50 percent in 1982, 38.5 percent in 1987 and 28 percent in 1988. It rose to 31 percent in 1991 and, under the 1993 budget act (OBRA 1993), to 39.6 percent in 1993. From 1988 to 1990 a 33 percent 'rate bubble' applied to part of the income range.
c-us8-reagan-rates.label: consensus

c-us8-reagan-scores.text: In the Treasury's estimates of revenue effects as a percentage of GDP, for each act's year of enactment and the three years after it, the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA) cut revenue by 1.21 percent of GDP in its year of enactment and by 2.60, 3.58 and 4.15 percent in the next three years, an average of 2.89 percent; the 1982 act (TEFRA) raised revenue by 0.53 percent in its year of enactment and by an average of 0.98 percent; the Tax Reform Act of 1986 raised it by 0.41 percent in its year of enactment and by an average of 0.01 percent; the 1990 budget act (OBRA 1990) raised it by 0.41 percent and by an average of 0.50 percent; and the 1993 budget act (OBRA 1993) raised it by 0.36 percent and by an average of 0.63 percent.
c-us8-reagan-scores.label: approx
c-us8-reagan-scores.note: Estimates by Jerry Tempalski of the Treasury's Office of Tax Analysis, for the year of enactment and the three following years, with their four-year average; they are estimates, not measured outcomes. 'Close to revenue-neutral', said of the 1986 act on this page, is this book's description of its average of 0.01 percent.

c-us8-reagan-tra.text: Signing the Tax Reform Act on 22 October 1986, Reagan said: 'Millions of working poor will be dropped from the tax rolls altogether'.
c-us8-reagan-tra.label: consensus

c-us8-reagan-volcker.text: Under Paul Volcker the Federal Reserve changed course in October 1979, choosing to 'target reserve growth rather than the fed funds rate as its policy instrument.'
c-us8-reagan-volcker.label: consensus

c-us8-reagan-recession.text: The federal funds rate peaked at 19.10 percent in June 1981. The economy 'entered recession again in July 1981', and unemployment reached 10.8 percent in November and December 1982; it was 5.3 percent in December 1988.
c-us8-reagan-recession.label: consensus

c-us8-reagan-inflation.text: In William Niskanen's figures inflation 'declined from 10.4 percent in 1980 to 4.2 percent in 1988.' Federal Reserve History gives an average of 'only 3.5 percent in the latter half of the 1980s.'
c-us8-reagan-inflation.label: approx
c-us8-reagan-inflation.note: The two sources use different periods, and possibly different price measures.

c-us8-reagan-debt.text: Federal debt held by the public rose from 24.9 percent of GDP in fiscal 1980 to 38.8 percent in fiscal 1989 and 40.4 percent in 1990. William Niskanen, using privately held debt, gives a rise 'from 22.3 percent of GDP to 38.1 percent.'
c-us8-reagan-debt.label: approx
c-us8-reagan-debt.note: Two different measures of federal debt: OMB's debt held by the public, and Niskanen's privately held debt.

c-us8-reagan-patco.text: When the air traffic controllers struck in 1981, Reagan said on 3 August that those who failed to report for duty 'are in violation of the law, and if they do not report for work within 48 hours, they have forfeited their jobs'. On 5 August 1981 he fired 'the 11,345 union employees who ignored his presidential order'.
c-us8-reagan-patco.label: consensus

c-us8-reagan-niskanen.text: William Niskanen, a member of Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, wrote that 'the major achievements of Reaganomics were the sharp reductions in marginal tax rates and in inflation'. On federal spending he wrote that there was 'no "Reagan revolution"'.
c-us8-reagan-niskanen.label: debated
c-us8-reagan-niskanen.note: The view of a participant who defends the tax and inflation record but not the spending record. Krugman and Friedman, on this page, are critics.

c-us8-reagan-krugman.text: Paul Krugman wrote in Peddling Prosperity (1994), as quoted in William Niskanen's review of the book: 'There was no sign of an acceleration of long-term growth rates at any point during the twelve years of conservative rule'.
c-us8-reagan-krugman.label: debated
c-us8-reagan-krugman.note: Known here only through a quotation in a review by Niskanen, himself a defender of Reaganomics; the passage was not seen in the book. The twelve years are those of Reagan and George H. W. Bush, 1981-1993. Niskanen, on this page, credits Reaganomics with lower tax rates and inflation.

c-us8-reagan-friedman.text: The Harvard economist Benjamin Friedman, author of Day of Reckoning: The Consequences of American Economic Policy under Reagan and After (Random House, 1988), drew six observations from the period in 'Learning From the Reagan Deficits' (NBER, March 1992), among them that 'Across-the-board cuts in personal income tax rates reduced the government's tax revenues', that 'Reducing tax revenues did not restrain government spending, at least not by enough to avoid the emergence of historically large deficits', and that 'Greater deficits did result in reduced private investment'.
c-us8-reagan-friedman.label: debated
c-us8-reagan-friedman.note: Friedman's own words, from the abstract of his 1992 working paper; three of its six observations are quoted. Niskanen, on this page, credits Reaganomics with lower tax rates and inflation.

c-us8-cw-buildup.text: The Reagan administration 'pursued a comprehensive modernization of U.S. nuclear and conventional forces.'
c-us8-cw-buildup.label: consensus

c-us8-cw-defshare.text: Computed from BEA data, national defense spending was about 6.4 percent of GDP in the third quarter of 1980, about 7.9 percent in the third quarter of 1986 and about 6.7 percent in the third quarter of 1991.
c-us8-cw-defshare.label: approx
c-us8-cw-defshare.note: This book's arithmetic: BEA's national defense consumption expenditures and gross investment divided by nominal GDP, both in billions of dollars at annual rates (for example 364.250 / 4,607.669 in 1986).

c-us8-cw-sdi.text: On 23 March 1983 Reagan proposed a missile defence aimed at 'rendering these nuclear weapons impotent and obsolete.' The Office of the Historian describes the Strategic Defense Initiative ('Star Wars') as a programme 'which Soviet leaders found highly threatening'.
c-us8-cw-sdi.label: consensus

c-us8-cw-reykjavik.text: At Reykjavik in October 1986 Reagan and Gorbachev 'discussed the prospect of abolishing all nuclear weapons.'
c-us8-cw-reykjavik.label: consensus

c-us8-cw-berlin.text: At the Brandenburg Gate on 12 June 1987 Reagan said: 'General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, if you seek liberalization: Come here to this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!'
c-us8-cw-berlin.label: consensus

c-us8-cw-drafts.text: Peter Robinson, the speechwriter, writes that the State Department and the National Security Council 'submitted their own alternate drafts', and that 'In each, the call to tear down the wall was missing.'
c-us8-cw-drafts.label: tradition
c-us8-cw-drafts.note: The speechwriter's own account, published by the National Archives in 2007.

c-us8-cw-inf.text: The INF Treaty, signed on 8 December 1987, banned ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometres. The Senate advised ratification on 27 May 1988, the treaty entered into force on 1 June 1988, and 'A total of 2,692 missiles was eliminated'. The Office of the Historian writes that it 'eliminated an entire class of missiles'.
c-us8-cw-inf.label: consensus

c-us8-cw-era.text: In Moscow in 1988 Reagan said that the term 'evil empire' belonged to 'another era.'
c-us8-cw-era.label: consensus

c-us8-cw-irancontra.text: Britannica describes the Iran-Contra affair as a scandal in which the National Security Council 'became involved in secret weapons transactions and other activities that either were prohibited by the U.S. Congress or violated the stated public policy of the government.' The Boland Amendment of 1984 'banned direct or indirect U.S. military aid to the Contras'. On 13 November 1986 Reagan told the nation: 'We did not—repeat—did not trade weapons or anything else for hostages, nor will we.' On 4 March 1987 he said: 'A few months ago I told the American people I did not trade arms for hostages. My heart and my best intentions still tell me that's true, but the facts and the evidence tell me it is not.'
c-us8-cw-irancontra.label: consensus

c-us8-cw-walsh.text: Independent Counsel Walsh reported that '14 persons were charged'; 11 were convicted, and 'two convictions were overturned on appeal', those of North and Poindexter. President George H. W. Bush pardoned six people on 24 December 1992. Walsh's final report is dated 4 August 1993.
c-us8-cw-walsh.label: consensus

c-us8-cw-nobel.text: Mikhail Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1990 'for the leading role he played in the radical changes in East-West relations'.
c-us8-cw-nobel.label: consensus

c-us8-cw-sempa.text: Francis Sempa, asking whether Reagan was a crusader or a conciliator, answers: 'The answer, I believe, is that he was both'. In his account 'Reagan the crusader launched a political, military, psychological, and economic offensive designed to undermine Soviet power', while 'Reagan the conciliator engaged in summitry and arms control negotiations with a reform-oriented Mikhail Gorbachev'. His essay summarises Peter Schweizer and Paul Kengor as seeing a deliberate strategy, and cites John Lewis Gaddis, who, Sempa writes, held that Reagan ended the Cold War by 'changing rather than containing' the Soviet Union.
c-us8-cw-sempa.label: debated
c-us8-cw-sempa.note: Sempa's own words; Schweizer, Kengor and Gaddis are given only as Sempa reports them. Brooks and Wohlforth stress material pressures, and English stresses ideas and Gorbachev's 'new thinkers'.

c-us8-cw-bw.text: Stephen Brooks and William Wohlforth (International Security, 2000/01) argue, as the Belfer Center's summary of their article puts it, that shifting material pressures 'had a much greater influence on Soviet foreign policy in the 1980s than previously thought.'
c-us8-cw-bw.label: debated
c-us8-cw-bw.note: Given through an editorial summary, not the authors' words. Sempa credits both Reagan's pressure and his negotiation; English, replying to them, stresses ideas.

c-us8-cw-english.text: Robert English replied in 'Power, Ideas, and New Evidence on the Cold War's End: A Reply to Brooks and Wohlforth' (2002); the Belfer Center's summary says he faults them for privileging materialist explanations 'to the exclusion of other possible causes—in particular, the influence of "new thinkers" led by Mikhail Gorbachev'.
c-us8-cw-english.label: debated
c-us8-cw-english.note: Given through an editorial summary, not English's own words. Brooks and Wohlforth, and Sempa, on this page, stress material pressures or Reagan's policies.

c-us8-bc-gulf.text: Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. A coalition 'Comprising forces from thirty-four countries' began the air war on 16 January 1991 and the ground war on 24 February; the war ended on 28 February.
c-us8-bc-gulf.label: consensus

c-us8-bc-gulfvotes.text: On 12 January 1991 the Senate passed S.J.Res.2, a joint resolution to authorize the use of United States armed forces under UN Security Council Resolution 678, by 52 to 47: Republicans 42 to 2 and Democrats 10 to 45. The House passed H.J.Res.77 by 250 to 183: Democrats 86 to 179 and Republicans 164 to 3.
c-us8-bc-gulfvotes.label: consensus

c-us8-bc-naftavotes.text: The House passed NAFTA on 17 November 1993 by 234 to 200 (Democrats 102 to 156, Republicans 132 to 43); the Senate passed it on 20 November 1993 by 61 to 38 (Democrats 27 to 28, Republicans 34 to 10).
c-us8-bc-naftavotes.label: consensus

c-us8-bc-nafta-gain.text: Caliendo and Parro estimate in their abstract that under NAFTA the 'U.S.'s welfare increases by 0.08%' and that intra-bloc trade increased by 41 percent for the United States.
c-us8-bc-nafta-gain.label: debated
c-us8-bc-nafta-gain.note: A model-based estimate of small national gains. Hakobyan and McLaren, on this page, find concentrated local losses.

c-us8-bc-nafta-loss.text: Hakobyan and McLaren find NAFTA 'dramatically lowering wage growth for blue-collar workers in the most affected industries and localities'.
c-us8-bc-nafta-loss.label: debated
c-us8-bc-nafta-loss.note: A finding about the places and industries most exposed, not the national average. Caliendo and Parro, on this page, estimate a small national gain.

c-us8-bc-contract.text: The Republicans' Contract with America was 'signed Sept. 27, 1994, on the Capitol steps'. Among its pledges was to 'require all laws that apply to the rest of the country also apply equally to the Congress'. Apart from term limits, all its parts were passed by the House, and Newt Gingrich became 'the first Republican in 40 years to serve as speaker'.
c-us8-bc-contract.label: consensus

c-us8-bc-welfare.text: Welfare reform, which President Clinton signed, became Public Law 104-193, approved on 22 August 1996. It replaced Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC) with Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), which now provides 'approximately $16.5 billion to states'.
c-us8-bc-welfare.label: consensus

c-us8-bc-haskins.text: Ron Haskins of the Brookings Institution, who from 1986 spent 14 years on the staff of the House Ways and Means Committee and wrote Work over Welfare: The Inside Story of the 1996 Welfare Reform Law (2006), told Congress in 2006 that 'Between 1994 and 2005, the caseload declined about 60 percent', and that 'child poverty fell every year' from 1994 to 2000.
c-us8-bc-haskins.label: debated
c-us8-bc-haskins.note: The case that the law succeeded, from a scholar who worked on it. Shaefer and Edin, on this page, find rising extreme poverty; Meyer and colleagues dispute their measure.

c-us8-bc-shaefer.text: Shaefer and Edin (Social Service Review, 2013) find in their abstract that the 'prevalence of extreme poverty has risen sharply since 1996, particularly among those most affected by the 1996 welfare reform.'
c-us8-bc-shaefer.label: debated
c-us8-bc-shaefer.note: The case that the law left a group in deep poverty. Haskins finds falling caseloads and child poverty; Meyer and colleagues dispute the measure.

c-us8-bc-meyer.text: Meyer, Wu, Mooers and Medalia, in an NBER working paper that links 2011 survey data to administrative records, reply that of households with survey-reported cash income below $2 a person a day 'more than 90% are not in extreme poverty once we include in-kind transfers, replace survey reports of earnings and transfer receipt with administrative records, and account for the ownership of substantial assets', and conclude that extreme poverty 'cannot be substantially higher now due to welfare reform, as many commentators have claimed.'
c-us8-bc-meyer.label: debated
c-us8-bc-meyer.note: A dispute about measurement: in-kind benefits, under-reported income and assets. Shaefer and Edin, on this page, report a sharp rise.

c-us8-bc-surplus.text: In OMB's series the federal budget ran a deficit of 4.45 percent of GDP in fiscal 1992 and 0.26 percent in 1997, surpluses of 0.76 percent in 1998, 1.30 in 1999, 2.30 in 2000 and 1.21 in 2001, and a deficit of 1.44 percent in 2002.
c-us8-bc-surplus.label: consensus

c-us8-bc-houseimp.text: On 19 December 1998 the House of Representatives adopted the first article of impeachment against President Clinton by 228 to 206 (Republicans 223 to 5, Democrats 5 to 200, the one independent against) and the third by 221 to 212 (Republicans 216 to 12, Democrats 5 to 199, the one independent against). The second article failed by 205 to 229 and the fourth by 148 to 285.
c-us8-bc-houseimp.label: consensus

c-us8-bc-impeach.text: In President Clinton's impeachment trial, on 12 February 1999, the Senate voted 45 guilty and 55 not guilty on Article I (perjury); all 45 guilty votes were Republican, and 10 Republicans voted not guilty. On Article II (obstruction) it voted 50 to 50; the five Republicans voting not guilty were Chafee, Collins, Jeffords, Snowe and Specter.
c-us8-bc-impeach.label: consensus

c-us8-imm-irca.text: Reagan signed the Immigration Reform and Control Act (IRCA) on 6 November 1986, writing: 'The employer sanctions program is the keystone and major element.' Applicants for legalization had to establish 'that they entered the United States before January 1, 1982', the act created a 'special agricultural worker adjustment program', and employers who hired unauthorized workers faced 'civil penalties of $250 to $10,000'.
c-us8-imm-irca.label: consensus

c-us8-imm-irca27.text: Bryan Baker of DHS's Office of Immigration Statistics wrote in October 2010: 'Nearly 2.7 million persons became LPRs under IRCA, including 1.6 million pre-1982s and 1.1 million SAWs', that is, about 1.6 million who had lived in the country since before 1982 and 1.1 million special agricultural workers.
c-us8-imm-irca27.label: approx
c-us8-imm-irca27.note: DHS's own rounded figures. LPRs are lawful permanent residents; SAWs are special agricultural workers, who did not have to have entered before 1982.

c-us8-imm-1990.text: Signing the Immigration Act of 1990 on 29 November 1990, President George H. W. Bush said: 'This bill is good for families, good for business, good for crime fighting, and good for America.' The act set 'a flexible cap of 700,000 until 1995 and 675,000 thereafter', created a lottery for '40,000 diversity visas', 'increased the number of annual employment visas from 54,000 to 140,000' and created Temporary Protected Status.
c-us8-imm-1990.label: consensus

c-us8-imm-census.text: Between the 2010 and 2020 censuses the Hispanic population grew 23 percent, from 50.5 million (16.3 percent of the population) to 62.1 million (18.7 percent); the Asian-alone population grew 35.5 percent, to 19.9 million, and the White-alone population fell 8.6 percent. The Census Bureau writes that comparisons of the 2020 and 2010 race data 'should be made with caution', and that differences in the overall racial distributions are 'largely due to improvements in the design of the two separate questions for race data collection and processing as well as some demographic changes over the past 10 years.'
c-us8-imm-census.label: approx
c-us8-imm-census.note: Part of the change reflects changed questions and coding of race and ethnicity, so the shifts are not purely demographic.

c-us8-imm-slow.text: The Census Bureau reported on 27 January 2026 that 'U.S. population growth slowed to 0.5%' between July 2024 and July 2025, as net international migration declined.
c-us8-imm-slow.label: consensus

c-us8-imm-pew.text: Pew Research Center (Passel and Krogstad, 21 August 2025) estimates that the unauthorized immigrant population 'reached an all-time high of 14 million in 2023 after two consecutive years of record growth', 4.1 percent of the population, above its previous high of 12.2 million in 2007. It adds that 'From January to June 2025, the unauthorized immigrant population likely declined, possibly by as much as 1 million.'
c-us8-imm-pew.label: approx
c-us8-imm-pew.note: A residual estimate from survey data, with a margin of error; the 2025 figure is preliminary.

c-us8-imm-dhs.text: The Department of Homeland Security's Office of Homeland Security Statistics estimated, as USAFacts reports it, that 11 million unauthorized immigrants were living in the United States on 1 January 2022, up from 8.46 million in 2000.
c-us8-imm-dhs.label: approx
c-us8-imm-dhs.note: DHS's own report could not be opened for this book; the figure is given as USAFacts (updated 28 July 2026) reports it.

c-us8-imm-mpi.text: The Migration Policy Institute (Gelatt, Ruiz Soto and Bachmeier, October 2025) estimates that the unauthorized population 'reached 13.7 million as of mid-2023', and that its growth, 'in 2025, may have even reversed.'
c-us8-imm-mpi.label: approx
c-us8-imm-mpi.note: An estimate with its own methods and reference date; the 2025 statement is a projection, not a count.

c-us8-imm-cbo.text: The Congressional Budget Office, on 7 January 2026, 'reduced its projections of net immigration from 2025 to 2029'.
c-us8-imm-cbo.label: consensus

c-us8-imm-mariel.text: Economists disagree about immigration's effect on the wages of the least-skilled, testing it on the 1980 Mariel boatlift to Miami. George Borjas finds in his abstract that 'The wage of high school dropouts in Miami dropped dramatically, by 10 to 30 percent'. Giovanni Peri and Vasil Yasenov, studying 'a sample of non-Cuban high-school dropouts', 'find no significant difference in the wages of workers in Miami relative to its control after 1980.'
c-us8-imm-mariel.label: debated
c-us8-imm-mariel.note: Both are NBER working papers on the same episode, using different samples and methods; each is given in its own abstract's words.

c-us8-imm-daca.text: Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) was announced on 15 June 2012. Applicants had to be 'under the age of 31 as of June 15, 2012', to have come to the United States before their 16th birthday, and to have 'continuously resided in the United States since June 15, 2007'.
c-us8-imm-daca.label: consensus

c-us8-imm-dacacourt.text: On 17 January 2025 the Fifth Circuit, reviewing the Texas district court's ruling 'that declared the DACA program to be unlawful', largely affirmed it but 'narrowed the ruling to apply only to Texas' (OSV News, 7 November 2025). CBS News reported on 30 September 2025 that 'As of the end of June, there were more than 525,000 people enrolled in DACA, with nearly 88,000 of them living in Texas', and that under the administration's plan 'Those residing in Texas will only be eligible for the program's deportation deferrals — not work authorization.'
c-us8-imm-dacacourt.label: consensus

c-us8-imm-dacanow.text: As consulted on 4 November 2026, USCIS's DACA page says it 'will continue to accept and process DACA renewal requests', and that it accepts initial requests but 'will not process initial DACA requests.' The Texas Tribune reported on 31 October 2025 that it was 'still unclear when, or if, Hanen will approve' the administration's plan; FWD.us, an advocacy group that supports DACA, wrote on 4 May 2026: 'We are still waiting on Judge Hanen to issue directions on how to implement this decision'.
c-us8-imm-dacanow.label: consensus

c-us8-imm-dacabacklog.text: CBS News (Julia Ingram and Lexi Salazar, 8 October 2026), citing federal data, reported that 'the number of active DACA holders declined by 14%, to 436,350, between September 2025 and June 30', and that 'the backlog of pending renewal applications has more than quadrupled over that timeframe, to over 125,000.'
c-us8-imm-dacabacklog.label: approx
c-us8-imm-dacabacklog.note: CBS attributes the figures to federal data without naming the dataset; the end date is 30 June 2026.

c-us8-imm-ice.text: ICE's budget explanation to Congress, as the Washington Times reported on 15 April 2026, gave 442,637 removals in fiscal 2025 (to 30 September 2025), 166,939 of them of people with criminal records other than illegal entry, and set a future annual target of '1,000,000 returns and removals.' Newsweek reported the same day, from DHS data, that ICE 'deported 442,637 individuals between October 2024 and September 2025.'
c-us8-imm-ice.label: approx
c-us8-imm-ice.note: An official figure, known here through two newspapers' reports of it.

c-us8-imm-dhsclaim.text: DHS said, as Fox News reported on 21 May 2026, that President Trump's first year back in office had seen more than 3 million people living in the country illegally leave, 'including an estimated 2.2 million "self-deportations"', and that nearly 900,000 had been deported as of 17 May 2026. The Migration Policy Institute likewise reports that 'DHS officials have claimed more than 3 million total departures'.
c-us8-imm-dhsclaim.label: approx
c-us8-imm-dhsclaim.note: DHS's own figures, as reported; DHS has not published a detailed enforcement report since January 2025, so they cannot be checked against one.

c-us8-imm-dhsoct.text: A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek (Dan Gooding, 13 October 2026): 'As of September, we have now deported nearly 1.1 million illegal aliens and arrested over 1.1 million illegal aliens.'
c-us8-imm-dhsoct.label: approx
c-us8-imm-dhsoct.note: DHS's own figure, as reported, in the department's own words; DHS has not published a detailed enforcement report since January 2025 against which to check it. MPI's and AP's figures are on this page.

c-us8-imm-mpideport.text: In Marc Rosenblum's analysis for the Migration Policy Institute (October 2026), 'ICE and CBP together completed about 980,000 total deportations' from 20 January 2025 to 31 July 2026, 'a figure in line with the department's public statements'. MPI estimates 'between 790,000 and 1.9 million total departures of immigrants with at least one year of U.S. residence (via deportation or self-departure)': about 480,000 deportations and between 310,000 and 1.5 million self-departures. If 'border turnarounds and other deportations of immigrants present for less than one year' are included, 'these additional 500,000 deportations would bring MPI's total estimate' to between 1.3 million and 2.4 million total departures. He notes that DHS's statistics office 'released its last detailed monthly enforcement report' in January 2025, writes that DHS's departure count 'likely includes certain lawfully present immigrants and U.S. citizens', and concludes that 'it is highly unlikely that 3 million immigrants have departed the United States via deportation or self-departure.'
c-us8-imm-mpideport.label: approx
c-us8-imm-mpideport.note: An independent estimate built from publicly available data, given as ranges for departures. DHS's higher figures are given on this page.

c-us8-imm-ap.text: The Associated Press (22 October 2026), reporting MPI's study, wrote that the administration 'is on track to deport about 660,000 people over the past year', 'a 26% increase from the yearly average from 2021 to 2024'; MPI gives this as a projection, writing that the administration 'was on track to complete 660,000 in FY 2026'. AP also reported that '69% of all deportations between Jan. 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026, were of people initially intercepted at the border'. It reported that the administration had released its own figures, 'including that 1.2 million migrants have been deported or removed during Trump's second term', and that 'The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.' White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: 'President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.'
c-us8-imm-ap.label: approx
c-us8-imm-ap.note: Official and independent figures for overlapping periods, as AP reported them; the 660,000 is a projection for fiscal 2026.

c-us8-imm-abc.text: ABC News (Luke Barr, 21 July 2026) reported: 'ICE currently has 65,765 individuals in detention facilities, 60% of whom have a criminal record, according to the agency.'
c-us8-imm-abc.label: approx
c-us8-imm-abc.note: ICE's own figure, as reported; the report does not define 'criminal record', a different measure from TRAC's count of convictions.

c-us8-imm-trac.text: TRAC reports that 'Immigration and Customs Enforcement held 65,765 in ICE detention according to data current as of July 11, 2026', and that 70.6 percent of them had no criminal conviction.
c-us8-imm-trac.label: approx
c-us8-imm-trac.note: TRAC's tabulation of ICE data at one date; detention numbers change daily.

c-us8-911-deaths.text: The attacks of 11 September 2001 'killed 2,977 people from 90 nations': 2,753 in New York, '184 people were killed at the Pentagon' and '40 people were killed on Flight 93'.
c-us8-911-deaths.label: consensus

c-us8-911-aumf.text: The Authorization for Use of Military Force (S.J.Res. 23, Public Law 107-40), approved on 18 September 2001, provides in section 2(a): 'That the President is authorized to use all necessary and appropriate force against those nations, organizations, or persons he determines planned, authorized, committed, or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001, or harbored such organizations or persons, in order to prevent any future acts of international terrorism against the United States by such nations, organizations or persons.'
c-us8-911-aumf.label: consensus

c-us8-911-aumfvote.text: The AUMF passed the Senate 98 to 0 on 14 September 2001 and the House 420 to 1: Republicans 214 to 0, Democrats 204 to 1 and independents 2 to 0; the one vote against was cast by Lee, a California Democrat.
c-us8-911-aumfvote.label: consensus

c-us8-911-patriot.text: The USA PATRIOT Act was approved on 26 October 2001. Its Title II is headed 'ENHANCED SURVEILLANCE PROCEDURES', and its section 215 'ACCESS TO RECORDS AND OTHER ITEMS UNDER THE FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE SURVEILLANCE ACT.'
c-us8-911-patriot.label: consensus

c-us8-911-patriotvote.text: The Patriot Act passed the House 357 to 66 on 24 October 2001 (Republicans 211 to 3, Democrats 145 to 62, independents 1 to 1) and the Senate 98 to 1 on 25 October; the one vote against in the Senate was Feingold's, a Wisconsin Democrat.
c-us8-911-patriotvote.label: consensus

c-us8-911-dhs.text: After 'the passage of the Homeland Security Act by Congress in November 2002', the Department of Homeland Security combined 'all or part of 22 different federal departments and agencies', 'opening its doors on March 1, 2003.'
c-us8-911-dhs.label: consensus

c-us8-911-iraq.text: The Iraq resolution (H.J.Res. 114, Public Law 107-243), approved on 16 October 2002, provides in section 3(a): 'The President is authorized to use the Armed Forces of the United States as he determines to be necessary and appropriate in order to-- (1) defend the national security of the United States against the continuing threat posed by Iraq; and (2) enforce all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions regarding Iraq.'
c-us8-911-iraq.label: consensus

c-us8-911-iraqvote.text: The House passed the Iraq resolution 296 to 133 on 10 October 2002: Republicans 215 to 6, Democrats 81 to 126 and the one independent against. The Senate passed it 77 to 23 on 11 October: Republicans 48 to 1 (Chafee voting no), Democrats 29 to 21 and the independent Jeffords against.
c-us8-911-iraqvote.label: approx
c-us8-911-iraqvote.note: The House party figures are the Clerk's; the Senate's are counted from its roll-call list. Some secondary sources give 82 Democratic yeas in the House; the Clerk gives 81.

c-us8-911-crs.text: The Congressional Research Service counted 'appropriations for the past 13 years of war that total $1.6 trillion' through fiscal year 2014: $815 billion (51 percent) for Iraq and $686 billion (43 percent) for Afghanistan and other counterterrorism operations.
c-us8-911-crs.label: approx
c-us8-911-crs.note: CRS counts appropriations for war operations through FY2014. Brown's Costs of War project counts wider and future costs and reaches a far larger total.

c-us8-911-cow.text: Neta C. Crawford (2021), of Boston University and a co-director of the Costs of War project at Brown University's Watson Institute, estimates the budgetary costs of the post-9/11 wars at 'about $8 trillion in current dollars' ($8,043 billion): $5,843 billion spent in fiscal years 2001 to 2022, including interest on war borrowing, increases in the base defence budget, homeland security and veterans' care, plus about $2.2 trillion in future obligations for veterans' care to fiscal 2050. The Defense Department's overseas contingency appropriations make up $2,101 billion of the total.
c-us8-911-cow.label: debated
c-us8-911-cow.note: Crawford counts costs beyond war appropriations, including interest, veterans' care and obligations to 2050; CRS counts appropriations for war operations only, $1.6 trillion through FY2014. The two totals answer different questions, and neither is a CBO estimate.

c-us8-911-gitmo.text: 'The prison opened on Jan 11, 2002, with the arrival of 20 detainees', and 'the US military has held about 780 men and boys there'. In January 2026 the New York Times counted 'The remaining 15 wartime prisoners', and on 3 September 2026 the Washington Examiner reported 15 remaining, 'as is still the case with the detention facility.'
c-us8-911-gitmo.label: approx
c-us8-911-gitmo.note: Counts from news reports, by Carol Rosenberg of the New York Times (January 2026) and the Washington Examiner (September 2026); 'about 780' is the reporter's round figure.

c-us8-911-migrants.text: In 2025 the base was also used to hold migrants: the New York Times counted 'about 775 migrants held there for days or weeks', and reported that 'As of Jan 9, Homeland Security held 54 men there'.
c-us8-911-migrants.label: approx
c-us8-911-migrants.note: A news report's figures; the total for migrants is approximate.

c-us8-911-ksm.text: On 11 July 2025 the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit voted 2 to 1 to throw out plea deals that 'stipulated life sentences without parole for Mohammed and two co-defendants'. On 19 October 2026 the Supreme Court 'declined to review former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin's decision to cancel plea agreements' for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid Bin 'Attash, leaving the lower-court ruling in place; 'Justice Brett Kavanaugh recused himself from consideration of the case.'
c-us8-911-ksm.label: consensus

c-us8-911-trial.text: In August 2026 a military judge set the trial of Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, Walid bin Attash, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali and Mustafa al-Hawsawi: 'The trial is scheduled to begin June 5, 2028, 18 months later than the January 2027 start that prosecutors had requested.' Steve Vladeck of Georgetown University Law Center, a CNN legal analyst who 'filed a friend-of-the-court brief urging the justices to take up the appeals', said that 'even the current summer 2028 trial date is entirely unrealistic given how many issues remain to be resolved.'
c-us8-911-trial.label: debated
c-us8-911-trial.note: The date is the military judge's, as reported by the Associated Press on 27 August 2026; the doubt is Vladeck's forecast, in a CNN wire story by John Fritze republished by Scripps News on 19 October 2026.

c-us8-gr-recession.text: The Great Recession 'began in December 2007 and ended in June 2009, which makes it the longest recession since World War II.' Real GDP 'fell 4.3 percent from its peak in 2007Q4 to its trough in 2009Q2'; home prices 'fell approximately 30 percent, on average, from their mid-2006 peak to mid-2009'; the net worth of households and nonprofit organisations fell from about $69 trillion in 2007 to $55 trillion in 2009; and the unemployment rate 'peaked at 10 percent in October 2009'.
c-us8-gr-recession.label: approx
c-us8-gr-recession.note: Federal Reserve History's figures; home prices and net worth are rounded averages, and the 10 percent peak is a monthly rate.

c-us8-gr-lehman.text: Lehman Brothers 'was forced to file for bankruptcy in September 2008', with 'a reported $639 billion in assets'. 'It was the largest bankruptcy in U.S. history at that time'.
c-us8-gr-lehman.label: consensus

c-us8-gr-tarpvote.text: The bill carrying the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), H.R. 3997, failed in the House on 29 September 2008, 205 to 228 (Democrats 140 to 95, Republicans 65 to 133). The Senate passed a revised bill, H.R. 1424, 74 to 25 on 1 October (Democrats 39 to 9, Republicans 34 to 15, independents 1 to 1), and the House passed it 263 to 171 on 3 October (Democrats 172 to 63, Republicans 91 to 108).
c-us8-gr-tarpvote.label: consensus

c-us8-gr-tarpcost.text: In its final report on TARP (April 2024) the Congressional Budget Office found that '$444 billion of the $700 billion initially authorized was disbursed' and that 'the government's total subsidy cost was $31 billion'. Mortgage programmes cost about $31 billion and aid to the auto industry about $12 billion, while purchases of bank capital gained about $9 billion and investment partnerships for securitization markets about $3 billion.
c-us8-gr-tarpcost.label: approx
c-us8-gr-tarpcost.note: CBO's final estimate; the programme figures are rounded.

c-us8-gr-vz.text: Pietro Veronesi and Luigi Zingales (2010) estimate that the October 2008 intervention 'increased the value of banks' financial claims by $130 billion' at 'a taxpayers' cost of $21-$44 billion'. They also write: 'The big winners of the plan were the bondholders of the three former investment banks and Citigroup, while the losers were JP Morgan shareholders and the US taxpayers.'
c-us8-gr-vz.label: debated
c-us8-gr-vz.note: From the paper's own abstract, which finds both a net gain in value and a distribution of gains and losses it criticises. CBO puts TARP's total cost at $31 billion.

c-us8-gr-arravote.text: The conference report on the stimulus bill (the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, H.R. 1) passed the House 246 to 183 on 13 February 2009 (Democrats 246 to 7, Republicans 0 to 176) and the Senate 60 to 38 the same day, with three Republicans, Collins, Snowe and Specter, voting yes.
c-us8-gr-arravote.label: consensus

c-us8-gr-arracbo.text: The Congressional Budget Office estimated in 2015 that the stimulus's 'total impact over the 2009-2019 period will amount to nearly $840 billion', and that its effects on output 'peaked in the first half of 2010.'
c-us8-gr-arracbo.label: approx
c-us8-gr-arracbo.note: CBO's estimate of the act's budgetary cost and its model-based judgement of its effects.

c-us8-gr-dfvote.text: Dodd-Frank passed the House 237 to 192 on 30 June 2010 (Democrats 234 to 19, Republicans 3 to 173) and the Senate 60 to 39 on 15 July 2010; the three Republicans voting yes were Brown, Collins and Snowe, and the one Democrat voting no was Feingold.
c-us8-gr-dfvote.label: consensus

c-us8-gr-unemp.text: The unemployment rate, annual averages (BLS, Current Population Survey): 2006 4.6 percent; 2007 4.6; 2008 5.8; 2009 9.3; 2010 9.6; 2011 8.9; 2012 8.1.
c-us8-gr-unemp.label: consensus

c-us8-gr-foreclose.text: RealtyTrac counted foreclosure filings on '2,824,674 U.S. properties in 2009', 'a 21 percent increase' from 2008 and 'a 120 percent increase' from 2007. In 2010 'A record 2.9 million properties received foreclosure filings.'
c-us8-gr-foreclose.label: approx
c-us8-gr-foreclose.note: A private-sector count of properties with any foreclosure filing, not of completed foreclosures.

c-us8-gr-romer.text: Before the act passed, Christina Romer of the Council of Economic Advisers and Jared Bernstein of the Office of the Vice-President estimated that a package of about $775 billion 'is expected to create between three and four million jobs by the end of 2010', and warned that such estimates 'are subject to significant margins of error.'
c-us8-gr-romer.label: debated
c-us8-gr-romer.note: A forecast made before the act passed, quoted here from an unsigned Joint Economic Committee commentary that criticises it. Taylor finds little direct effect from the stimulus packages of the 2000s; Chodorow-Reich finds a national multiplier, absent a monetary-policy response, of 1.7 or above.

c-us8-gr-taylor.text: John B. Taylor (2011) finds that the stimulus packages of the 2000s 'had little if any direct impact on consumption or government purchases', and that 'Households largely saved the transfers and tax rebates.'
c-us8-gr-taylor.label: debated
c-us8-gr-taylor.note: From the paper's own abstract. Chodorow-Reich and, before passage, Romer and Bernstein argue for substantial effects.

c-us8-gr-cr.text: Gabriel Chodorow-Reich (2019), reviewing geographic cross-sectional evidence, puts the cross-sectional spending multiplier at about 1.8 and concludes that the evidence points to 'a national no-monetary-policy-response multiplier of 1.7 or above.'
c-us8-gr-cr.label: debated
c-us8-gr-cr.note: From the paper's own abstract. Taylor finds that the 2000s packages 'had little if any direct impact on consumption or government purchases'.

c-us8-gr-igm.text: In the Clark Center's IGM panel of economists (29 July 2014), 36 agreed or strongly agreed and 1 disagreed that the stimulus had lowered unemployment at the end of 2010; on whether its benefits would exceed its costs, 25 agreed, 10 were uncertain and 2 disagreed.
c-us8-gr-igm.label: approx
c-us8-gr-igm.note: Counted from the panel's published answers; a survey of academic economists' opinions, not a measurement.

c-us8-obama-elec.text: In the 2008 election Barack Obama won 69,498,516 votes (52.93 percent) and 365 electoral votes, and John McCain 59,948,323 (45.65 percent) and 173.
c-us8-obama-elec.label: approx
c-us8-obama-elec.note: The Federal Election Commission's official counts; the American Presidency Project gives slightly different totals (69,456,897 for Obama).

c-us8-obama-acavote.text: The Affordable Care Act (H.R. 3590) passed the Senate 60 to 39 on 24 December 2009, every Republican present voting no (Bunning did not vote). On 21 March 2010 the House concurred 219 to 212: Democrats 219 to 34, Republicans 0 to 178.
c-us8-obama-acavote.label: consensus

c-us8-obama-acacbo.text: The Congressional Budget Office and the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated on 20 March 2010 that enacting H.R. 3590 as passed by the Senate together with the reconciliation proposal (H.R. 4872) 'would produce a net reduction in federal deficits of $143 billion over the 2010–2019 period'.
c-us8-obama-acacbo.label: approx
c-us8-obama-acacbo.note: CBO and JCT's estimate made before enactment, of the two bills together.

c-us8-obama-elec2012.text: In the 2012 election, by the Federal Election Commission's count, Barack Obama won 65,915,795 votes (51.06 percent) and 332 electoral votes, and Mitt Romney 60,933,504 (47.20 percent) and 206.
c-us8-obama-elec2012.label: consensus

c-us8-obama-jobs.text: In the BLS series (via FRED, last updated 2 October 2026) the unemployment rate was 7.8 percent in January 2009, peaked at 10.0 percent in October 2009 and was 4.7 percent in January 2017.
c-us8-obama-jobs.label: approx
c-us8-obama-jobs.note: Current estimates; BLS revises seasonally adjusted figures in later releases.

c-us8-obama-census.text: By the Census Bureau's Current Population Survey, the uninsured were '13.3 percent or 41.8 million' in 2013 and 10.4 percent in 2014, and '8.8 percent, or 28.1 million' in 2016. In 2024 '92.0 percent or 310 million' had coverage, so 8.0 percent did not.
c-us8-obama-census.label: approx
c-us8-obama-census.note: Survey estimates from the Census Bureau; the 2024 uninsured share is 100 minus the 92.0 percent covered.

c-us8-obama-nhis.text: By the CDC's National Health Interview Survey (all ages, uninsured at the time of interview): 2020 9.7 percent; 2021 9.2; 2022 8.4; 2023 7.6; 2024 8.2. In 2025 the uninsured were '8.3% of Americans of all ages (28.0 million people)'.
c-us8-obama-nhis.label: approx
c-us8-obama-nhis.note: Survey estimates from a different survey from the Census Bureau's, so the two series do not match exactly.

c-us8-obama-mjw.text: Sarah Miller, Norman Johnson and Laura Wherry, comparing near-elderly adults 'most likely to benefit', identified 'using survey information on socioeconomic status', in states with and without the ACA's Medicaid expansions, find that 'prior to the ACA expansions, mortality rates across expansion and non-expansion states trended similarly', and that 'Individuals in expansion states experienced a 0.132 percentage point decline in annual mortality, a 9.4 percent reduction over the sample mean, as a result of the Medicaid expansions.'
c-us8-obama-mjw.label: debated
c-us8-obama-mjw.note: From the authors' own abstract, on the Medicaid expansions only. CBO's 2014 projection of fewer hours worked concerns a different effect of the law.

c-us8-obama-cbo.text: In February 2014 the Congressional Budget Office projected that the ACA would reduce hours worked 'on net, by about 1.5 percent to 2.0 percent' from 2017 to 2024, equal to 'a decline in the number of full-time-equivalent workers of about 2.0 million in 2017', rising to 'about 2.5 million in 2024', 'almost entirely because workers will choose to supply less labor.'
c-us8-obama-cbo.label: debated
c-us8-obama-cbo.note: CBO's projection of the law's effect on labour supply. Miller, Johnson and Wherry measure a different effect, on mortality.

c-us8-obama-tp.text: Theda Skocpol and Vanessa Williamson (2011), as their book is summarised on a page of Harvard's Weatherhead Center, describe the Tea Party as joining grassroots activists with national elites and funders, who used grassroots energy to further long-standing goals.
c-us8-obama-tp.label: debated
c-us8-obama-tp.note: A summary of the book, not the authors' own words. Tea Party Patriots' own statement of its values is given beside it.

c-us8-obama-tpp.text: The organisation Tea Party Patriots names, on its current website, 'our three core values of fiscal responsibility, constitutionally limited government, and free markets.'
c-us8-obama-tpp.label: debated
c-us8-obama-tpp.note: The organisation's own current statement of its values, not a finding; Skocpol and Williamson's account is given beside it.

c-us8-obama-house.text: Party divisions in the House at the start of each Congress: 111th Democrats 257, Republicans 178; 112th (after the 2010 midterm) Democrats 193, Republicans 242; 113th Democrats 201, Republicans 234; 114th (after the 2014 midterm) Democrats 188, Republicans 247.
c-us8-obama-house.label: consensus

c-us8-obama-oberg.text: In Obergefell v. Hodges (26 June 2015), decided 5 to 4, Justice Kennedy wrote for the Court: 'The Court now holds that same-sex couples may exercise the fundamental right to marry.' He also wrote that there is 'no lawful basis for a State to refuse to recognize a lawful same-sex marriage performed in another State'. Of the petitioners Kennedy wrote: 'They ask for equal dignity in the eyes of the law.'
c-us8-obama-oberg.label: consensus

c-us8-obama-dissent.text: Chief Justice Roberts, joined by Justices Scalia and Thomas, wrote the lead dissent, and Scalia, Thomas and Alito each also wrote a dissent. Roberts wrote: 'But this Court is not a legislature. Whether same-sex marriage is a good idea should be of no concern to us.' He also wrote: 'Under the Constitution, judges have power to say what the law is, not what it should be.'
c-us8-obama-dissent.label: consensus

c-us8-obama-davis.text: On 10 November 2025 the Supreme Court denied Kim Davis's petition asking it to overrule Obergefell, with no noted dissent; SCOTUSblog observed that if any justices disagreed, 'they did not note that disagreement publicly.'
c-us8-obama-davis.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-elec2016.text: In the 2016 election, by the Federal Election Commission's count, Hillary Clinton won 65,853,514 votes (48.18 percent) and Donald Trump 62,984,828 (46.09 percent), a margin of 2,868,686 for Clinton. The electors cast 304 votes for Trump and 227 for Clinton. Seven electors voted for others; in Texas '1 was cast for John Kasich; 1 was cast for Ron Paul'.
c-us8-t1-elec2016.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-tcja.text: The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (H.R. 1) passed the Senate 51 to 48 in the early hours of 20 December 2017, every Republican present voting yes and no Democrat or independent doing so, and the House 224 to 201 later that day, Republicans 224 to 12 and Democrats 0 to 189.
c-us8-t1-tcja.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-tcjacbo.text: The Congressional Budget Office and the staff of the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated in December 2017 that the act would 'increase the deficit by $1,455 billion over the next 10 years, excluding effects from macroeconomic feedback'. In September 2025 CBO found its estimates 'consistent with observed outcomes in 2018 and 2019'.
c-us8-t1-tcjacbo.label: approx
c-us8-t1-tcjacbo.note: CBO's estimate made before enactment, leaving out macroeconomic feedback; its 2025 review covers 2018 and 2019 only.

c-us8-t1-tcjainv.text: Gabriel Chodorow-Reich, Matthew Smith, Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick (2024) find that 'Domestic investment of firms with the mean tax change increases 20% versus a no-change baseline', and that 'the tax revenue feedback from growth offsets only 2p.p. of the direct cost of 41% of pre-TCJA corporate revenue.'
c-us8-t1-tcjainv.label: debated
c-us8-t1-tcjainv.note: From the paper's own abstract; 'p.p.' means percentage points. CBO's deficit estimate leaves out macroeconomic feedback.

c-us8-t1-steel.text: Proclamation 9705 of 8 March 2018 imposed 'a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on steel articles'.
c-us8-t1-steel.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-china.text: On 22 March 2018 the U.S. Trade Representative found under Section 301 that China's technology-transfer practices were 'unreasonable and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce'.
c-us8-t1-china.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-ard.text: Mary Amiti, Stephen Redding and David Weinstein (2019) find that 'the full incidence of the tariffs has fallen on domestic consumers and importers so far'.
c-us8-t1-ard.label: debated
c-us8-t1-ard.note: From the paper's own abstract. The administration's case for action against China rested on USTR's Section 301 finding of 'unreasonable' practices.

c-us8-t1-adbh.text: David Autor, Anne Beck, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson (2024) find that 'The trade-war has not to date provided economic help to the US heartland', and also that exposed regions 'became less likely to identify as Democrats'.
c-us8-t1-adbh.label: debated
c-us8-t1-adbh.note: From the paper's own abstract, which reports an economic and a political effect. The administration's case rested on USTR's Section 301 finding.

c-us8-t1-usitc.text: The U.S. International Trade Commission (2023) found that the Section 232 tariffs 'increased U.S. production of steel products by 1.9 percent', that 'U.S. production of steel was $1.3 billion higher in 2021 due to section 232 tariffs', and that the steel and aluminum tariffs together 'decreased production in downstream industries 0.6 percent on average.' Michael Stumo of the Coalition for a Prosperous America, an advocacy group that describes itself as 'exclusively representing domestic producers and workers', said on the day of the study that 'tariffs are a critical reshoring tool to stimulate domestic production'.
c-us8-t1-usitc.label: debated
c-us8-t1-usitc.note: The Commission's model-based estimates, and an advocacy group's reading of them. Amiti, Redding and Weinstein, and Autor and co-authors, find costs to domestic buyers and no economic help to exposed regions.

c-us8-t1-judges.text: Pew Research Center counts 226 judges appointed in Trump's single term, against 320 for Obama and 322 for George W. Bush over two terms each, among them 3 Supreme Court justices and '54 federal appellate judges in four years, one short of the 55 Obama appointed'. Pew counts only 'the three main tiers of the federal court system' and 'excludes those appointed to certain specialized courts, such as the U.S. Court of International Trade.' Ballotpedia counts '234 Article III federal judges through December 31, 2020', including 174 district judges, and lists the Court of International Trade among Article III courts.
c-us8-t1-judges.label: approx
c-us8-t1-judges.note: Pew (226) counts the Supreme Court, appeals and district courts only; Ballotpedia (234) counts all Article III judges, including the Court of International Trade. Neither source reconciles the two totals.

c-us8-t1-house.text: Party divisions in the House at the start of each Congress: 115th Democrats 194, Republicans 241; 116th (after the 2018 midterm) Democrats 235, Republicans 199, with one seat vacant because North Carolina had not certified the election in its Ninth District.
c-us8-t1-house.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-imp1.text: On 18 December 2019 the House impeached Trump. Article I (abuse of power) passed 230 to 197, with no Republican voting yes and Democrats voting 229 to 2; Article II (obstruction of Congress) passed 229 to 198.
c-us8-t1-imp1.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-acq1.text: On 5 February 2020 the Senate acquitted: 48 guilty to 52 not guilty on Article I, Romney the only Republican voting guilty, and 47 to 53 on Article II.
c-us8-t1-acq1.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-imp2.text: On 13 January 2021 the House impeached Trump a second time, on an article headed 'incitement of insurrection' (H. Res. 24), 232 to 197, with 10 Republicans voting yes. On 13 February 2021 the Senate voted 57 to 43 to convict, short of the two-thirds required; the seven Republicans voting guilty were Burr, Cassidy, Collins, Murkowski, Romney, Sasse and Toomey.
c-us8-t1-imp2.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-covid.text: The CDC counted '350,831 COVID-19 deaths' in 2020 in which COVID was the underlying cause. Counting deaths with COVID-19 as underlying or contributing cause, the toll was 384,536 in 2020 and, provisionally, 460,513 in 2021.
c-us8-t1-covid.label: approx
c-us8-t1-covid.note: Death-certificate counts; the total depends on whether COVID-19 is counted only as the underlying cause or also as a contributing one. The 2021 figure is provisional: 'provisional data for 2021 are incomplete'.

c-us8-t1-jobs.text: In the BLS series (via FRED, last updated 2 October 2026) the unemployment rate was 4.7 percent in January 2017, 3.5 percent in February 2020, 14.8 percent in April 2020 and 6.4 percent in January 2021. In BEA's annual series (via FRED, last updated 30 September 2026) real GDP grew 2.5 percent in 2017, 3.0 percent in 2018 and 2.6 percent in 2019, and fell 2.1 percent in 2020.
c-us8-t1-jobs.label: approx
c-us8-t1-jobs.note: Current estimates; BEA and BLS revise these series in later releases.

c-us8-t1-cares.text: The CARES Act (H.R. 748) passed the Senate 96 to 0 on 25 March 2020 and was 'signed into law on March 27, 2020'. The Congressional Budget Office and the staff of the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated that it would 'increase federal deficits by about $1.7 trillion over the 2020-2030 period'.
c-us8-t1-cares.label: approx
c-us8-t1-cares.note: The vote and the date are records; the deficit figure is a preliminary estimate by CBO and JCT.

c-us8-t1-vax.text: On 11 December 2020 the Food and Drug Administration 'issued the first emergency use authorization (EUA) for a vaccine for the prevention of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)'.
c-us8-t1-vax.label: consensus

c-us8-t1-elec2020.text: In the 2020 election, by the Federal Election Commission's count, Joe Biden won 81,283,501 votes (51.31 percent) and Donald Trump 74,223,975 (46.85 percent), a margin of 7,059,526; the electoral vote was 306 to 232.
c-us8-t1-elec2020.label: consensus

c-us8-j6-senate.text: The report of the Senate Homeland Security and Rules committees (released 8 June 2021), from what they called 'a joint bipartisan oversight investigation', concerns 'the security, planning, and response failures' of 6 January 2021. It opens: 'On January 6, 2021, the world witnessed a violent and unprecedented attack on the U.S. Capitol'. It records that 'Members of Congress were scheduled to perform their constitutional obligation to count the electoral votes'; that 'Most demonstrators headed to the Ellipse, near the White House, for the "Save America" rally'; that 'At approximately 12:53 p.m., individuals within that group picked up one of the metal bike racks'; that 'Rioters, attempting to disrupt the Joint Session of Congress, broke into the Capitol building'; that 'Vice President Pence and congressional leaders were evacuated to secure locations'; that the D.C. National Guard 'began arriving at the Capitol Complex at 5:20 p.m.', 'more than four hours after the barriers at the Capitol were first breached'; that 'Approximately 140 law enforcement officers reported injuries suffered during the attack'; that 'seven individuals, including three law enforcement officers, ultimately lost their lives'; and that, after the Senate reconvened at 8:00 p.m. and the House at about 9:00 p.m., 'the Joint Session of Congress officially affirmed the results of the Electoral College at 3:42 a.m. on January 7.'
c-us8-j6-senate.label: approx
c-us8-j6-senate.note: The report's own figures; 'approximately' is its word for the injury count and the time.

c-us8-j6-house.text: The final report of the House select committee on the January 6th attack (H. Rept. 117-663, 22 December 2022) states that 'the central cause of January 6th was one man, former President Donald Trump, whom many others followed. None of the events of January 6th would have happened without him.'
c-us8-j6-house.label: debated
c-us8-j6-house.note: The committee's conclusion, quoted from the official report on Congress.gov; PBS NewsHour reproduced the report. The proclamation of 20 January 2025 and a December 2024 interim report of the House Administration subcommittee chaired by Barry Loudermilk frame the events and the select committee differently.

c-us8-j6-cha.text: An interim report of the Committee on House Administration's Subcommittee on Oversight, chaired by Barry Loudermilk (December 2024), states: 'The January 6 Select Committee was improperly constituted and lacked authority.'
c-us8-j6-cha.label: debated
c-us8-j6-cha.note: A Republican-led subcommittee's conclusion about the earlier, Democratic-led inquiry; an argument, not a court finding.

c-us8-j6-schumer.text: On 21 January 2025 Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, said on the Senate floor: 'There is no other way to describe President Trump's pardon of Jan. 6 offenders than un-American.'
c-us8-j6-schumer.label: debated
c-us8-j6-schumer.note: An opponent's characterisation, as reported by The Hill; the proclamation's own words state the case for the pardons.

c-us8-j6-doj.text: The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia reported that 'Approximately 1,583 have been federally charged with crimes associated with the attack of the U.S. Capitol'; 'Approximately 608 have been charged with assaulting resisting, or impeding law enforcement agents or officers'; 'Approximately 1,100 defendants have had their cases fully adjudicated and received sentences'; and 'There are 170 defendants who have either pled guilty or been found guilty at trial' and were awaiting sentencing.
c-us8-j6-doj.label: approx
c-us8-j6-doj.note: The office's page is undated; ABC News reported the charge figures on 6 January 2025.

c-us8-j6-pardon.text: President Trump's proclamation of 20 January 2025 states: 'This proclamation ends a grave national injustice that has been perpetrated upon the American people over the last four years and begins a process of national reconciliation.' It commutes 'the sentences of the following individuals', fourteen in all (Rhodes, Meggs, Harrelson, Caldwell, Watkins, Minuta, Vallejo, Moerschel, Hackett, Nordean, Biggs, Rehl, Pezzola and Bertino), 'to time served as of January 20, 2025'; grants 'a full, complete and unconditional pardon to all other individuals convicted of offenses related to events that occurred at or near the United States Capitol on January 6, 2021'; and directs the Attorney General to 'pursue dismissal with prejudice to the government of all pending indictments.'
c-us8-j6-pardon.label: consensus

c-us8-j6-babbitt.text: In May 2025 the Justice Department agreed in principle to pay 'a little under $5 million' to the family of Ashli Babbitt, who was shot by a Capitol Police lieutenant. U.S. Capitol Police Chief J. Thomas Manger, in a message to his officers, wrote: 'This is extremely disappointing and I completely disagree with the Department of Justice's decision', and 'In 2021, the DOJ said that there was no evidence to show that law enforcement broke the law.'
c-us8-j6-babbitt.label: consensus

c-us8-j6-sub.text: Rep. Barry Loudermilk, a Georgia Republican, chairs 'a congressional subcommittee reinvestigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol.' Its first hearing was titled 'Examining the Investigation into the DNC and RNC Pipe Bombs'. NPR, checking claims made at the hearing, reported that 'The president has direct control of the D.C. National Guard', and that a Department of Justice inspector general report found no evidence 'showing or suggesting that the FBI had undercover employees in the various protest crowds, or at the Capitol, on January 6.' Brian Cole Jr. was charged with 'placing two pipe bombs, which never exploded', and, NPR reported in January 2026, 'has pleaded not guilty.' In July 2026 'All parties agreed Wednesday to a Feb. 16, 2027, trial date for Brian Cole'. The Washington Examiner reported on 1 October 2026 that 'A federal grand jury returned an eight-count indictment Wednesday that charged Cole separately for each bomb', and that 'Cole was in court on Thursday for his arraignment'.
c-us8-j6-sub.label: consensus

c-us8-j6-anniv.text: On the fifth anniversary, Loudermilk said: 'True accountability requires focusing on facts, not selective storytelling for partisan gain.' A White House website blamed the Capitol Police for turning a 'peaceful demonstration into chaos.' Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, said: 'Donald Trump and far-right extremists in Congress have repeatedly attempted to rewrite history.'
c-us8-j6-anniv.label: debated
c-us8-j6-anniv.note: Each side's own words, as reported by Reuters in January 2026; these are arguments, not findings.

c-us8-j6-polls.text: In a Marist poll of 7-9 January 2025, before the proclamation, 62 percent disapproved and 35 percent approved of pardoning people 'convicted of attacking the Capitol'; Republicans approved 64 to 30 percent, and 89 percent of Democrats disapproved. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll of 20-21 January 2025, 58 percent said 'that Trump should not pardon all people convicted'. As reported by the Christian Science Monitor, Washington Post-University of Maryland polls found that the share saying punishments were 'not harsh enough' fell from more than half in 2021 to 38 percent in 2023, and that in December 2024 90 percent of Democrats and 40 percent of Republicans opposed pardons.
c-us8-j6-polls.label: approx
c-us8-j6-polls.note: Polls, each with a sampling margin and its own wording; Marist's was taken before the proclamation and Reuters/Ipsos's just after it.

c-us8-biden-arp.text: The Senate passed the American Rescue Plan (H.R. 1319) on 6 March 2021 by 50 votes to 49, with no Republican voting yes ('Republicans: 0 Yea, 49 Nay, 1 Not Voting'). The House agreed on 10 March 2021 by '220 Yea, 211 Nay': Democrats voted 220-1 and Republicans 0-210.
c-us8-biden-arp.label: consensus

c-us8-biden-arp-cbo.text: CBO's estimate of 10 March 2021 for H.R. 1319 as passed by the Senate on 6 March 2021 gives 'Estimated Effects on the Deficit' of $1,855,603 million over 2021-2030 and $1,844,112 million over 2021-2031: increases in deficits of about $1.86 trillion and $1.84 trillion.
c-us8-biden-arp-cbo.label: approx
c-us8-biden-arp-cbo.note: A projection made before enactment; CBO gives its figures in millions of dollars, and the rounding to trillions is this book's.

c-us8-biden-jobs.text: In the BLS series (via FRED, last updated 2 October 2026) the unemployment rate was 6.4 percent in January 2021, reached 3.4 percent in April 2023, its lowest between January 2021 and January 2025, and was 4.0 percent in January 2025. In BEA's annual series (via FRED, last updated 30 September 2026) real GDP grew 6.3 percent in 2021, 2.4 percent in 2022, 2.9 percent in 2023 and 3.0 percent in 2024.
c-us8-biden-jobs.label: approx
c-us8-biden-jobs.note: Current estimates; BEA and BLS revise these series in later releases.

c-us8-biden-cpi-gap.text: The BLS reports that it 'did not collect CPI data from October 1, 2025, through November 12, 2025', the period of the 2025 federal government shutdown, and that 'Missing CPI data affected October and November 2025 indexes'. The BLS CPI-U series on FRED has no value for October 2025.
c-us8-biden-cpi-gap.label: approx
c-us8-biden-cpi-gap.note: The 2025 annual average shown here is the BLS figure as published by the Minneapolis Fed.

c-us8-biden-afg-review.text: The State Department's after-action review of the withdrawal from Afghanistan (released June 2023) states that 'The decisions of both President Trump and President Biden to end the U.S. military mission in Afghanistan' 'had serious consequences for the viability of the Afghan government and its security.' It adds: 'Those decisions are beyond the scope of this review, but the AAR team found that during both administrations' 'there was insufficient senior-level consideration of worst-case scenarios and how quickly those might follow.'
c-us8-biden-afg-review.label: debated
c-us8-biden-afg-review.note: The State Department's own review, set beside Biden's account of the evacuation; Axios reported it on 30 June 2023.

c-us8-biden-cpi.text: Annual percent change in the consumer price index (CPI-U, annual averages): 2019, 1.8; 2020, 1.2; 2021, 4.7; 2022, 8.0; 2023, 4.1; 2024, 2.9; 2025, 2.6.
c-us8-biden-cpi.label: approx
c-us8-biden-cpi.note: BLS CPI-U annual averages as published by the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis; other inflation measures give different figures.

c-us8-biden-peak.text: The BLS reported that consumer prices rose 9.1 percent in the 12 months to June 2022, 'the largest 12-month increase since the period ending November 1981', and 2.9 percent in the 12 months to December 2024.
c-us8-biden-peak.label: consensus

c-us8-biden-bb.text: Ben Bernanke and Olivier Blanchard (2025) conclude that, 'contrary to early concerns that inflation would be spurred by overheated labor markets, most of the inflation surge resulted from shocks to prices given wages'. Their abstract adds that tight labor markets have had a more persistent effect on wage growth and inflation.
c-us8-biden-bb.label: debated
c-us8-biden-bb.note: Bernanke and Blanchard weight price shocks most; the San Francisco Fed economists Jordà, Liu, Nechio and Rivera-Reyes estimate that fiscal support added about 3 points to US inflation by the end of 2021. The two findings measure different things and can both hold.

c-us8-biden-frbsf.text: Economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco (Jordà, Liu, Nechio and Rivera-Reyes, 28 March 2022) estimated that US fiscal support measures 'may have contributed to this divergence', US inflation running above that of other developed countries, 'by raising inflation about 3 percentage points by the end of 2021'. They wrote that the estimate was made 'with considerable uncertainty because the available sample is too short for any greater precision.' They added: 'Our estimates fall in the upper range of findings from other recent research.'
c-us8-biden-frbsf.label: debated
c-us8-biden-frbsf.note: The authors place their estimate in the upper range of other research; Bernanke and Blanchard (2025) find that most of the surge came from price shocks.

c-us8-biden-iija.text: The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (H.R. 3684) passed the Senate 69-30 on 10 August 2021, with 19 Republicans voting yes, and the House 228-206 on 5 November 2021, with 13 Republicans voting yes and 6 Democrats voting no.
c-us8-biden-iija.label: consensus

c-us8-biden-iija-cbo.text: NBC News reported in August 2021 that the Congressional Budget Office estimated the infrastructure bill would, 'On net', 'add $256 billion to projected deficits' over ten years.
c-us8-biden-iija-cbo.label: approx
c-us8-biden-iija-cbo.note: A news report of CBO's estimate, made before the bill was final.

c-us8-biden-chips.text: The CHIPS and Science bill (H.R. 4346) passed the Senate 64-33 on 27 July 2022, with 17 Republicans voting yes, and the House 243-187 on 28 July 2022, with 24 Republicans voting yes.
c-us8-biden-chips.label: consensus

c-us8-biden-chips-cbo.text: The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget reported on 22 July 2022 that CBO estimated the CHIPS bill would 'increase budget deficits by $48 billion over five years and by $79 billion through 2031'.
c-us8-biden-chips-cbo.label: approx
c-us8-biden-chips-cbo.note: CRFB's report of CBO's estimate, made before final passage.

c-us8-biden-ira.text: The Inflation Reduction Act (H.R. 5376) passed the Senate 51-50 on 7 August 2022, the Vice President breaking a 50-50 tie, and the House 220-207 on 12 August 2022. Both votes followed party lines.
c-us8-biden-ira.label: consensus

c-us8-biden-ira-cbo.text: CBO's estimate of the enacted law (Public Law 117-169), published on 7 September 2022, was a 'net decrease in the unified deficit totaling $58.1 billion over the 2022-2031 period'. CBO's cost estimate adds that the law's increased funding for tax enforcement 'also will increase revenues', that 'revenues will increase by $180 billion over the 2022-2031 period' as a result, and that under guidelines agreed to by the legislative and executive branches 'that change is not included in this cost estimate'.
c-us8-biden-ira-cbo.label: approx
c-us8-biden-ira-cbo.note: A projection made at enactment; actual effects depend on later spending, tax credits claimed and revenue collected. Adding the two gives about $238 billion; that sum is this book's arithmetic, not a CBO total.

c-us8-biden-abbey.text: On 26 August 2021 an ISIS-K bombing at Abbey Gate, Kabul, 'killed at least 160 Afghan civilians and 13 U.S. servicemembers', according to U.S. Central Command's investigation briefing of 4 February 2022.
c-us8-biden-abbey.label: consensus

c-us8-biden-aug31.text: On 31 August 2021 President Biden said: 'We completed one of the biggest airlifts in history, with more than 120,000 people evacuated to safety.' He spoke of 'The extraordinary success of this mission', said 'Thirteen heroes gave their lives', and declared: 'I was not going to extend this forever war, and I was not extending a forever exit.'
c-us8-biden-aug31.label: consensus

c-us8-biden-ukraine.text: On 20 April 2024 the House passed the Ukraine Security Supplemental (H.R. 8035) 311-112; Democrats voted 210-0 and Republicans 101 yes to 112 no. On 23 April 2024 the Senate cleared the combined foreign-aid package (H.R. 815) 79-18, with 31 Republicans voting yes and 15 no.
c-us8-biden-ukraine.label: consensus

c-us8-biden-2024.text: In the certified 2024 result Donald Trump received 77,302,580 votes (49.80 percent) and 312 electoral votes; Kamala Harris received 75,017,613 votes (48.32 percent) and 226 electoral votes.
c-us8-biden-2024.label: consensus

c-us8-t2-eo.text: According to the Federal Register, President Trump 'signed 225 Executive orders' in 2025, numbered 'from EO 14147 through EO 14371.'
c-us8-t2-eo.label: consensus

c-us8-t2-learning.text: In Learning Resources v. Trump (20 February 2026) the Supreme Court held, 6-3, that 'IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs', striking down the 'trafficking' tariffs on Canada, Mexico and China and the worldwide 'reciprocal' tariffs. Chief Justice Roberts wrote for the Court; Justice Kavanaugh, joined by Thomas and Alito, dissented, arguing that statutory text, history and precedent show that IEEPA authorizes tariffs.
c-us8-t2-learning.label: debated
c-us8-t2-learning.note: 6-3. The majority read the statute as not reaching tariffs; the dissent found clear authorization. The doctrine is set out in US2.13.

c-us8-t2-122.text: After the ruling the President imposed a 10% surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows surcharges for up to 150 days at a maximum rate of 15%. It applied to goods entered 'for consumption on or after 12:01 a.m. EST on Feb. 24' 2026. On 21 February the President said on social media that he would raise the rate 'to 15 percent'; STR reported on 24 February that 'no action to effectuate that change had been taken as of press time', Barnes Richardson on 27 February that 'For the time being, 10% is in Proclamation 11012', and Troutman Pepper Locke in October 2026 described 'a 10% worldwide tariff under Section 122' that 'ran from February 24 through July 24, 2026.' On 7 May 2026 the Court of International Trade held, 2-1, that the proclamation improperly invoked Section 122, granting relief only to three plaintiffs; the Federal Circuit stayed that judgment pending appeal on 11 June 2026. The Section 122 duties expired on 24 July 2026.
c-us8-t2-122.label: approx
c-us8-t2-122.note: Appeal status as of Troutman Pepper Locke's report of 12 October 2026; no Federal Circuit ruling was found.

c-us8-t2-301.text: New tariffs under Section 301, of 10% or 12.5% on imports from 60 trading partners, took effect on 24 July 2026. In a sample case challenging Section 301 tariffs, 'The panel heard argument on September 30, 2026'; as of 12 October 2026 'No decision has been issued, and the duties remain in effect.'
c-us8-t2-301.label: approx
c-us8-t2-301.note: Status as of Troutman Pepper Locke's report of 12 October 2026; no ruling was found.

c-us8-t2-refund.text: CBO estimates that about $130 billion was refunded during fiscal year 2026 for tariffs collected under IEEPA, and that customs duties fell from $195 billion in fiscal 2025 to $172 billion in fiscal 2026.
c-us8-t2-refund.label: approx
c-us8-t2-refund.note: CBO's monthly review of 8 October 2026 gives estimates for the year just ended, before final Treasury figures.

c-us8-t2-tariff-burden.text: Mary Amiti, Chris Flanagan, Sebastian Heise and David E. Weinstein of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York wrote on 12 February 2026: 'We find that nearly 90 percent of the tariffs' economic burden fell on U.S. firms and consumers.' As Yahoo Finance reported, the National Economic Council director, Kevin Hassett, told CNBC on 18 February 2026: 'I think it's the worst paper I've ever seen in the history of the Federal Reserve System', and said of the authors: 'They're basically only looking at changes in prices.'
c-us8-t2-tariff-burden.label: debated
c-us8-t2-tariff-burden.note: The New York Fed economists put most of the 2025 burden on Americans; the administration rejects their method; Caroline Freund, as the Tax Foundation reports, finds a larger share borne abroad.

c-us8-t2-tariff-freund.text: The Tax Foundation (Erica York and Alex Durante, 1 September 2026) reported that a study of the 2025 tariffs by the trade economist Caroline Freund finds that 'foreigners have absorbed 47 percent of the tariff burden while US importers paid 53 percent', a lower share for importers than other recent studies had found.
c-us8-t2-tariff-freund.label: debated
c-us8-t2-tariff-freund.note: The Tax Foundation's summary of Freund's paper; the New York Fed economists put nearly 90 percent of the burden on U.S. firms and consumers.

c-us8-t2-tariff-cea.text: A White House release of 8 July 2025 reported a Council of Economic Advisers analysis: 'This analysis suggests that tariffs have not reduced the disinflationary impulse from imported goods as of May.' The CEA acknowledged that its analysis 'does not identify the counterfactual in which tariffs are not instituted.'
c-us8-t2-tariff-cea.label: debated
c-us8-t2-tariff-cea.note: The administration's own economists, writing in mid-2025; the independent estimates of 2026 on this page find costs to U.S. households.

c-us8-t2-tariff-cost.text: The Budget Lab at Yale (24 July 2026): 'We estimate the ultimate consumer price impact of current-law tariff policy to be about 0.7%', and 'Estimated household costs due to tariffs total about $1,100 annually under current law.' The Tax Foundation (Erica York and Alex Durante, updated 10 September 2026): 'we estimate the tariffs will increase taxes by an average of $820 per US household' in 2026, and 'the new tariffs will reduce long-run GDP by 0.4 percent.'
c-us8-t2-tariff-cost.label: approx
c-us8-t2-tariff-cost.note: Model estimates that depend on which tariffs are in force; the Tax Foundation's long-run figure covers the tariffs it treats as permanent (under Sections 232, 301 and 338).

c-us8-t2-deport.text: The Migration Policy Institute (Marc R. Rosenblum, October 2026) counts that ICE and CBP 'completed about 980,000 total deportations between January 20, 2025, and July 31, 2026'. It reports that 'DHS officials have claimed more than 3 million total departures', including 'about 2 million unauthorized immigrant self-departures', a figure 'approximately double MPI's estimate' for self-departures.
c-us8-t2-deport.label: debated
c-us8-t2-deport.note: Official claims and an independent estimate, each attributed. MPI's deportation count and DHS's departure claim measure different things: departures include people who left on their own, whose number can only be estimated.

c-us8-t2-workforce.text: A Pew Research Center analysis of Office of Personnel Management data (13 March 2026) found that 'The federal workforce shrank by 10.3% in 2025, or a net of nearly 238,000 workers', from 2,312,301 in December 2024 to 2,074,649 in December 2025. 'The OPM dataset covers civilian federal workers only.'
c-us8-t2-workforce.label: approx
c-us8-t2-workforce.note: OPM data omit Congress, the judiciary, the Postal Service and some other agencies, so they cover most but not all civilian federal employment.
