c-us8-t2-gao.text: The Government Accountability Office (17 June 2026) found that across 22 agencies 'the total workforce across these agencies declined by nearly 256,000 employees', more than 11 percent, from December 2024 to January 2026; 'nearly 378,000 employees separated from these agencies during 2025' while they 'hired a total of about 127,000 employees'. Agencies offered 'incentives for employees to voluntarily resign or retire', carried out reductions in force and restricted hiring, and many who left had taken a deferred resignation offer.
c-us8-t2-gao.label: approx
c-us8-t2-gao.note: GAO's period (to January 2026) and its 22-agency scope differ from Pew's OPM-based comparison of December 2024 with December 2025.

c-us8-t2-leave.text: The Office of Personnel Management, answering press coverage of a GAO report, quoted it: 'GAO estimates that agencies spent about $9.5 billion on all paid administrative leave in 2025' and 'attributes about $6.7 billion of that to DRP', the deferred resignation program. OPM replied: 'So, for a one-time expense of at most $9.5 billion, taxpayers save more than $40 billion each year', a figure it reached by multiplying a rough average cost of about $150,000 per employee by the roughly 270,000 employees by which, it says, the government has shrunk.
c-us8-t2-leave.label: debated
c-us8-t2-leave.note: GAO's figures as OPM quotes them (this book could not open the GAO report, GAO-26-108477); the $40 billion is OPM's own calculation.

c-us8-t2-pps.text: Government Executive reported on 13 April 2026 that the Partnership for Public Service estimated that the administration's federal workforce changes had cost the economy 'more than $165.6 billion', including about $94.6 billion from cancelled grants at science agencies, valued with an NIH estimate of economic return per dollar, and about $53.2 billion attributed to disengaged civil servants. Its data director, Brandon Lardy, said 'this is a conservative estimate'.
c-us8-t2-pps.label: debated
c-us8-t2-pps.note: An estimate, mostly modelled, by a good-government group that has criticized the changes; administration officials argue that downsizing is needed to reduce federal spending.

c-us8-t2-doge.text: The Washington Examiner reported on 23 November 2025 that the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) had closed about eight months before its planned end, under the headline 'DOGE closes eight months early, but principles remain "alive and well"'.
c-us8-t2-doge.label: consensus

c-us8-t2-obbba.text: CBO estimated on 21 July 2025 that Public Law 119-21, the 2025 budget reconciliation act, will result in 'a net increase in the unified budget deficit' 'totaling $3.4 trillion over the 2025-2034 period', from 'a decrease in direct spending of $1.1 trillion' and 'a decrease in revenues of $4.5 trillion'.
c-us8-t2-obbba.label: approx
c-us8-t2-obbba.note: A ten-year projection against CBO's January 2025 baseline; actual effects will depend on the economy and later law.

c-us8-t2-cea-obbba.text: The Council of Economic Advisers (25 June 2025) projected '$2.1 to $2.3 trillion in offsetting deficit reduction due to higher growth from the OBBB tax provisions', assuming a '4.6 to 4.9 percent higher level of real GDP' over four years, 'about 1.1 to 1.2 percent higher average growth per year'. The White House said on 30 June 2025 that a score 'inclusive of economic growth' showed 'deficit reduction of $755 billion relative to the CBO's tax hike baseline'.
c-us8-t2-cea-obbba.label: debated
c-us8-t2-cea-obbba.note: Administration estimates that assume faster growth than CBO's; CBO estimates that the law increases deficits by $3.4 trillion over 2025-2034.

c-us8-t2-uninsured.text: As reported by Edwin Park of Georgetown's Center for Children and Families (14 August 2025), CBO found that the law 'will increase the number of uninsured people by 10 million in 2034'; the Medicaid work reporting requirement alone 'would increase the number of uninsured by 5.3 million in 2034 (before interactions).'
c-us8-t2-uninsured.label: debated
c-us8-t2-uninsured.note: CBO's projection as reported by Georgetown CCF; Christopher Jacobs (The Federalist) disputes that one Medicaid provision, Section 71114 (about 100,000 people), should be counted as increasing the uninsured.

c-us8-t2-jacobs.text: Christopher Jacobs, writing in The Federalist (14 August 2025), argued that one Medicaid provision counted in CBO's estimate, Section 71114, to which CBO attributed about 100,000 of the increase in the uninsured, 'didn't take anything away from anyone, or any state, now', and that the idea it would 'increase the uninsured' 'seems, if not laughable, at least highly speculative.' Of the work requirement he wrote that 'a community engagement requirement for program recipients seems reasonable.' He did not contest CBO's figures for the work requirement or for the limits on immigrants' eligibility, which he defended.
c-us8-t2-jacobs.label: debated
c-us8-t2-jacobs.note: Jacobs disputes about 100,000 of CBO's 10 million; Georgetown CCF's Edwin Park reports CBO's estimate as it stands.

c-us8-t2-shutdown.text: A government shutdown, 'The longest government shutdown in history', ended on Wednesday 12 November 2025 'after 43 days and more than a dozen attempts to reopen the government'. Democrats made 'the expiring health insurance tax credits' under the Affordable Care Act 'their key demand'; Republicans held that health care 'should be negotiated outside the context of funding the government'. The deal secured 'a vote in December on the Affordable Care Act tax credits'.
c-us8-t2-shutdown.label: consensus

c-us8-t2-aca.text: Axios reported that on 11 December 2025 'The Senate Democratic proposal, which would have extended the enhanced subsidies for three years, failed 51-48', and that the Republican alternative 'also failed on a vote of 51-48'; 60 votes were needed. On 8 January 2026 the House passed a three-year extension: 'In a 230 to 196 vote, 17 Republicans joined all Democrats in favor of the measure' (CBS News). KFF wrote on 30 October 2026: 'In 2026, the enhanced premium tax credits expired'.
c-us8-t2-aca.label: approx
c-us8-t2-aca.note: Status as described by KFF on 30 October 2026, before the status line of 2 November 2026.

c-us8-t2-gdp.text: BEA's advance estimate of 29 October 2026: real GDP 'increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026'; 'In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent.'
c-us8-t2-gdp.label: approx
c-us8-t2-gdp.note: An advance estimate, which BEA will revise.

c-us8-t2-jobs.text: The BLS reported on 2 October 2026 that in September 2026 'Total nonfarm payroll employment changed little in September (+29,000)', and 'Both the unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, changed little'.
c-us8-t2-jobs.label: approx
c-us8-t2-jobs.note: Monthly payroll figures are revised in later releases.

c-us8-t2-cpi.text: The BLS reported on 14 October 2026: 'The all items index rose 3.7 percent for the 12 months ending September', and 'The all items less food and energy index rose 2.6 percent over the year'.
c-us8-t2-cpi.label: consensus

c-us8-t2-midterms.text: The 2026 midterm general elections, for all 435 House seats among other offices, were set for 3 November 2026 ('The general elections will be held on Nov. 3'). They were held that day; this book's status line is 'as of 2 November 2026', and it reports no results.
c-us8-t2-midterms.label: consensus

c-us8-econ-psz.text: Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman (2018), combining tax, survey and national-accounts data, find that pretax income 'has stagnated for the bottom 50% of the distribution at about $16,000 a year', while 'Income has boomed at the top.'
c-us8-econ-psz.label: debated
c-us8-econ-psz.note: Piketty, Saez and Zucman find a large rise in top shares; Auten and Splinter (2024) find top shares lower, rising less, and little changed after tax.

c-us8-econ-as.text: Gerald Auten and David Splinter (2024) argue that 'Estimates of top income shares based only on individual tax returns are biased by tax-base changes', 'social changes, and missing income sources'. Adjusting for these, they find that top income shares 'are lower and have increased less since 1980 than other studies using tax data', with 'little change in aftertax top income shares', and that 'increasing government transfers and tax progressivity have resulted in rising real incomes for all income groups.'
c-us8-econ-as.label: debated
c-us8-econ-as.note: Auten and Splinter's adjustments for tax-base changes and missing income lower the rise in top shares; Piketty, Saez and Zucman find that income boomed at the top while the bottom half stagnated.

c-us8-econ-epi.text: The Economic Policy Institute reports that 'From 1979 to 2020, net productivity rose 61.8%', while 'the hourly pay of typical workers grew far slower—increasing only 17.5% over four decades', pay being 'the average compensation (wages and benefits) of production and nonsupervisory workers.'
c-us8-econ-epi.label: debated
c-us8-econ-epi.note: EPI finds a wide gap between productivity and typical pay; Feldstein (2008) found that total compensation per hour tracked productivity when both are deflated the same way; Stansbury and Summers (2017) find a link that persists but is offset by other factors.

c-us8-econ-feldstein.text: Martin Feldstein (2008) found that productivity in the nonfarm business sector doubled between 1970 and 2006, and that 'Wages, or more accurately total compensation per hour, increased at approximately the same annual rate during that period', when compensation is adjusted for inflation in the same way as output.
c-us8-econ-feldstein.label: debated
c-us8-econ-feldstein.note: Feldstein measures total compensation (including benefits) with the same price index as output; EPI compares typical workers' pay with net productivity.

c-us8-econ-ss.text: Anna Stansbury and Lawrence Summers (2017) find that over 1973-2016 'one percentage point higher productivity growth has been associated with 0.7 to 1 percentage points higher median' compensation growth, and conclude that 'other factors orthogonal to productivity have been acting to suppress typical compensation'.
c-us8-econ-ss.label: debated
c-us8-econ-ss.note: A middle position between EPI's gap and Feldstein's tracking: productivity still lifts typical pay, but other forces have held it down.

c-us8-econ-adh.text: David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson (2013) find that, between 1990 and 2007, rising Chinese 'import competition explains one-quarter of the contemporaneous aggregate decline in US manufacturing employment'. In a 2021 follow-up they report that the effects of the China shock 'are present out to 2019'.
c-us8-econ-adh.label: debated
c-us8-econ-adh.note: Autor, Dorn and Hanson compare local labor markets more and less exposed to Chinese imports; Caliendo, Dvorkin and Parro (2019) model the whole economy and find a smaller job loss with aggregate gains; Bloom, Handley, Kurmann and Luck (2019) find the losses concentrated in large firms that expanded non-manufacturing jobs.

c-us8-econ-cdp.text: Lorenzo Caliendo, Maximiliano Dvorkin and Fernando Parro (2019), using a general-equilibrium model, estimate that the China trade shock 'resulted in a reduction of about 0.55 million U.S. manufacturing jobs', 'about 16% of the observed decline in manufacturing employment from 2000 to 2007', and that 'The U.S. gains in the aggregate', though effects 'vary across U.S. labor markets.'
c-us8-econ-cdp.label: debated
c-us8-econ-cdp.note: A smaller estimate than Autor, Dorn and Hanson's, from a model of the whole economy rather than a comparison of local areas.

c-us8-econ-bloom.text: Nicholas Bloom, Kyle Handley, André Kurmann and Philip Luck (2019) find that the manufacturing job losses linked to Chinese imports were concentrated in 'large, importing firms that simultaneously expand employment in non-manufacturing.'
c-us8-econ-bloom.label: debated
c-us8-econ-bloom.note: A qualification of the China-shock findings: some losses in manufacturing were offset within the same firms.

c-us8-econ-mfg.text: The BLS reported in 2020 that 'In June 1979, manufacturing employment reached an all-time peak of 19.6 million'. In FRED's seasonally adjusted BLS series (read 4 November 2026), manufacturing employment was 19,553 thousand in June 1979, 19,282 in January 1980, 18,009 in January 1985, 17,797 in January 1990, 17,262 in January 1995, 17,284 in January 2000, 14,257 in January 2005, 14,004 in January 2007, 11,439 in February 2010, 12,265 in January 2015, 12,745 in January 2020, 11,382 in April 2020 and 12,652 in September 2026.
c-us8-econ-mfg.label: approx
c-us8-econ-mfg.note: Monthly BLS estimates, revised from time to time; the latest months are preliminary.

c-us8-econ-union.text: The BLS reports that the union membership rate 'was 10.0 percent in 2025', with 14.7 million members; 'In 1983, the first year for which comparable data are available, the union membership rate was 20.1 percent and there were 17.7 million union members.' In 2025 the public-sector rate was 32.9 percent and the private-sector rate 5.9 percent.
c-us8-econ-union.label: consensus

c-us8-econ-health.text: CMS reports that 'U.S. health care spending grew 7.2 percent in 2024, reaching $5.3 trillion or $15,474 per person', and that health spending accounted for 18.0 percent of GDP.
c-us8-econ-health.label: consensus

c-us8-faith-pew2014.text: Pew reported in June 2014 that the share of Americans with consistently liberal or consistently conservative views 'has doubled over the past two decades from 10% to 21%.'
c-us8-faith-pew2014.label: consensus

c-us8-faith-pew2022.text: Pew reported in August 2022: 'Today, 72% of Republicans regard Democrats as more immoral, and 63% of Democrats say the same about Republicans.' In 2016 the figures were 47 percent of Republicans and 35 percent of Democrats.
c-us8-faith-pew2022.label: consensus

c-us8-faith-congress.text: Pew (Drew DeSilver, March 2022), using DW-NOMINATE, 'a method that uses lawmakers' roll-call votes to place them in a two-dimensional ideological space', found that 'Democrats and Republicans are farther apart ideologically today than at any time in the past 50 years', and that 'both parties in both the House and the Senate have shifted further away from the center, but Republicans more so.'
c-us8-faith-congress.label: consensus

c-us8-faith-rls.text: Pew's 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study, 'conducted in English and Spanish from July 17, 2023, to March 4, 2024' among '36,908 respondents', found that 62 percent of adults identify as Christians, against 78 percent in 2007 and 71 percent in 2014; the unaffiliated 'stands at 29% in the new RLS, up from 23% in 2014 and 16% in 2007.' Between 2019 and 2024 the Christian share was 'relatively stable, hovering between 60% and 64%.'
c-us8-faith-rls.label: consensus

c-us8-faith-level.text: Pew's executive summary says that 'the religiously unaffiliated population, after rising rapidly for decades, has leveled off – at least temporarily.'
c-us8-faith-level.label: debated
c-us8-faith-level.note: That the share has held steady since about 2019 is Pew's finding; whether the plateau lasts is open, as Pew's own 'at least temporarily' signals.

c-us8-faith-groups.text: In the 2023-24 study 40 percent of adults are Protestant and 19 percent Catholic; 'Evangelical Protestants now make up 23% of U.S. adults, down from 26%', and 'Mainline Protestants account for 11% of U.S. adults, down from 18%'; Pew's report gives the base year: 'down from 26% in 2007' and 'down from 18% in 2007'; '2% are Jewish, and 1% each are Muslim, Buddhist or Hindu (all figures are rounded).'
c-us8-faith-groups.label: consensus

c-us8-faith-catholics.text: Pew reports that 'the Catholic population is 54% White, 36% Hispanic, 4% Asian and 2% Black.'
c-us8-faith-catholics.label: consensus

c-us8-faith-vote24.text: Pew's study of validated 2024 voters (26 June 2025) found that among white evangelical Protestants '81% voted for Trump in 2024, compared with 83% in 2020'; Trump took '55% of the Catholic vote to Harris' 43%'; and unaffiliated voters went '70% voting for Harris and 28% voting for Trump.'
c-us8-faith-vote24.label: consensus

c-us8-faith-jews.text: Pew estimated in 2021 that 'the 2020 Jewish population estimate is approximately 7.5 million, including 5.8 million adults and 1.8 million children', and that '2.4% of U.S. adults are Jewish'. Among Jewish adults '71% said they were Democrats or leaned Democratic', while '75% of Orthodox Jews said they were Republicans or leaned Republican'.
c-us8-faith-jews.label: approx
c-us8-faith-jews.note: A survey-based estimate; the count depends on how Jewish identity is defined.

c-us8-faith-fbi24.text: FBI figures as reported by the ADL (5 August 2025): 'reported single-bias anti-Jewish hate crime incidents rose to 1,938 incidents' in 2024, 'nearly 70 percent of all reported religion-based hate crimes', 'the highest number ever recorded by the FBI since it began collecting data in 1991'.
c-us8-faith-fbi24.label: approx
c-us8-faith-fbi24.note: The ADL's summary of FBI data; FBI totals depend on which law-enforcement agencies report.

c-us8-faith-fbi25.text: FBI figures as reported by the ADL (17 August 2026): 'A total of 1,528 anti-Jewish hate crime incidents were reported in 2025', 'accounting for 63 percent of the 2,408 religion-motivated hate crime incidents'. As reported by the Algemeiner (18 August 2026), Muslims 'were the victims of 205 hate crime incidents'. The FBI's own summary for 2025 reports that hate crime incidents 'decreased from 11,679 to 10,881', and that among 'agencies reporting 6 or more common months of hate crime data to the FBI's UCR Program for both 2024 and 2025', 'reported hate crime incidents decreased 7.0% from 11,404 in 2024 to 10,606 in 2025.'
c-us8-faith-fbi25.label: approx
c-us8-faith-fbi25.note: The bias-level figures are the ADL's and the Algemeiner's summaries of FBI data, since this book could not open the FBI's own tables; the totals are from the FBI's summary, which draws on 85.9 percent of agencies enrolled in its program. FBI totals depend on which agencies report.

c-us8-faith-adl.text: The ADL's audit (6 May 2026) counted '6,274 incidents of antisemitic assault, harassment and vandalism in 2025', a '33-percent decrease from 2024'; AP reported the 2024 total as 'the record-high 9,354 incidents'. '203 incidents were categorized as assault, an increase of 4 percent compared to 2024 (196 incidents).' The audit 'includes both criminal and non-criminal acts of harassment, vandalism and assault', 'as reported to ADL by victims, law enforcement, the media and partner organizations'.
c-us8-faith-adl.label: approx
c-us8-faith-adl.note: The ADL's own count, which includes non-criminal acts and so is not comparable with FBI hate-crime data; its criteria are debated (see the AP report).

c-us8-faith-adl-debate.text: AP reported that 'Some critics say the ADL's criteria is too broad', and that the counting has fueled 'an intense and divisive debate among American Jews and others'. Aryeh Tuchman, who 'formerly led the ADL's Center on Extremism' and now directs the Nexus Center for Antisemitism, which AP describes as 'a watchdog group that promotes a more nuanced definition of antisemitism than the ADL uses', told AP that the ADL's approach reflects a genuine concern that anti-Zionism threatens the safety of American Jews, and that many people disagree with that view.
c-us8-faith-adl-debate.label: debated
c-us8-faith-adl-debate.note: Critics hold that the ADL counts too much as antisemitism; the ADL's approach rests on the view, as Tuchman described it, that anti-Zionism threatens American Jews' safety. Tuchman's view is paraphrased from the AP report.

c-us8-faith-gallup.text: Gallup (Lydia Saad, 13 July 2026) found that 27 percent of Americans have 'a great deal' or 'quite a lot' of confidence in the core institutions it tracks on average, 'one percentage point above the record-low average in 2023', with 'Republicans now 13 points more confident in U.S. institutions than Democrats are' (36 percent against 23). Confidence stood at 67 percent for small business, 61 for the military, 45 for the police, 33 for organized religion, 27 each for the Supreme Court and the presidency, and 9 for Congress.
c-us8-faith-gallup.label: consensus

pages.title: The modern republic
pages.lede: In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series real GDP grew about 3.3 times between 1980 and 2025 while the population grew by about half, so real GDP per person rose about 2.2 times. Real median household income was about 41 percent higher in 2025 than in 1984, with falls after 2007 and after 2019, and federal debt held by the public rose from 24.9 percent of GDP in 1980 to 97.8 percent in 2025.
body: In the Bureau of Economic Analysis's series real GDP was $7,257.3 billion in 1980 and $23,943.3 billion in 2025, in chained 2017 dollars: about 3.3 times as large. It dipped in 2020, to $20,284.5 billion from $20,715.7 billion in 2019. [[c-us8-ov-gdp]] The population, also from BEA, rose from 227,726 thousand to 341,944 thousand, from about 228 million to about 342 million. [[c-us8-ov-pop]] Computed from BEA data, real GDP per person was about $31,900 in 1980 and about $70,000 in 2025, about 2.2 times as much. [[c-us8-ov-percap]]

The Census Bureau's real median household income, in what the series labels '2025 C-CPI-U Dollars', was $61,910 in 1984, the series' first year, and $87,460 in 2025, about 41 percent higher. Its path was uneven: $74,810 in 2007, $69,070 in 2012, $85,320 in 2019 and $81,460 in 2022. [[c-us8-ov-income]] On the Great Recession, see US8.6; on inflation in 2021-2024, US8.10; on inequality and wages, US8.12.

Federal debt held by the public, in the Office of Management and Budget's fiscal-year series, was 24.9 percent of GDP in 1980, 40.4 percent in 1990 and 47.2 percent in 1995. It fell to 31.4 percent in 2001, [[c-us8-ov-debt]] after the budget ran surpluses in fiscal 1998-2001 (US8.3), [[c-us8-bc-surplus]] and then rose to 52.1 percent in 2009, 98.3 percent in 2020 and 97.8 percent in 2025. [[c-us8-ov-debt]] On the federal purse and the Federal Reserve, see US2.13.

This chapter follows Reagan and the economy (US8.1), the American side of the end of the Cold War (US8.2), Bush and Clinton (US8.3) and immigration and a changing population (US8.4); then 9/11 at home (US8.5), the Great Recession at home (US8.6), Obama (US8.7), Trump's first term (US8.8), January 6 and its aftermath (US8.9), Biden (US8.10), Trump's second term to November 2026 (US8.11), the economy since 1980 (US8.12) and faith and polarization (US8.13). On the end of the Cold War worldwide, see 15.14 and 16.1; on 9/11 and the wars, 16.3; on the financial crisis, 16.4; on parties, money and polarization, US2.14.

pages.title: Reagan and the economy
pages.lede: Ronald Reagan won the 1980 election with 489 electoral votes, and the top income-tax rate fell from 70 percent in 1981 to 28 percent in 1988 while debt held by the public rose from 24.9 percent of GDP in 1980 to 40.4 percent in 1990. After the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker changed course in 1979, the federal funds rate peaked at 19.10 percent in June 1981, recession began in July 1981 and inflation, in William Niskanen's figures, fell from 10.4 percent in 1980 to 4.2 percent in 1988; economists such as Niskanen, who served on Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, and Paul Krugman have disagreed about what Reaganomics achieved.
body: In the 1980 election Ronald Reagan won 489 electoral votes and 50.7 percent of the popular vote; Jimmy Carter won 49 electoral votes and 41.0 percent, and John Anderson (independent) 6.6 percent. [[c-us8-reagan-1980]] The top federal income-tax rate was 70 percent in 1981, 50 percent in 1982, 38.5 percent in 1987 and 28 percent in 1988; it rose again to 31 percent in 1991 and 39.6 percent in 1993. From 1988 to 1990 a 33 percent 'rate bubble' also applied to part of the income range. [[c-us8-reagan-rates]] In the Treasury's estimates, the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 cut revenue by 1.21 percent of GDP in its year of enactment and by 4.15 percent in the third year after enactment; the 1982 act raised revenue by an average of about 1 percent of GDP a year over four years, and the Tax Reform Act of 1986 was close to revenue-neutral, with an average of 0.01 percent. [[c-us8-reagan-scores]] Signing the 1986 act on 22 October, Reagan said: 'Millions of working poor will be dropped from the tax rolls altogether'. [[c-us8-reagan-tra]]

Under Paul Volcker the Federal Reserve had changed course in October 1979, choosing to 'target reserve growth rather than the fed funds rate as its policy instrument.' [[c-us8-reagan-volcker]] The federal funds rate peaked at 19.10 percent in June 1981; the economy 'entered recession again in July 1981', and unemployment reached 10.8 percent in November and December 1982; it was 5.3 percent in December 1988. [[c-us8-reagan-recession]] In Niskanen's figures inflation 'declined from 10.4 percent in 1980 to 4.2 percent in 1988', and Federal Reserve History gives an average of 'only 3.5 percent in the latter half of the 1980s.' [[c-us8-reagan-inflation]] On the inflation of the 1970s, see US7.12; on the Federal Reserve, US2.13.

Federal debt held by the public rose from 24.9 percent of GDP in fiscal 1980 to 38.8 percent in fiscal 1989 and 40.4 percent in 1990; Niskanen, measuring privately held debt, gives a rise 'from 22.3 percent of GDP to 38.1 percent.' [[c-us8-reagan-debt]] When the air traffic controllers struck in 1981, Reagan said on 3 August that those who failed to report for duty 'are in violation of the law, and if they do not report for work within 48 hours, they have forfeited their jobs', and on 5 August he fired 'the 11,345 union employees who ignored his presidential order'. [[c-us8-reagan-patco]]

What did Reaganomics achieve? William Niskanen, a member of Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers, wrote that 'the major achievements of Reaganomics were the sharp reductions in marginal tax rates and in inflation', while finding that on federal spending there was 'no "Reagan revolution"'. [[c-us8-reagan-niskanen]] Paul Krugman, in Peddling Prosperity (1994), wrote, as Niskanen's review of the book quotes him, that 'There was no sign of an acceleration of long-term growth rates at any point during the twelve years of conservative rule' under Reagan and Bush. [[c-us8-reagan-krugman]] Benjamin Friedman of Harvard, author of Day of Reckoning (1988), drew lessons from the Reagan deficits in a 1992 paper, among them that 'Across-the-board cuts in personal income tax rates reduced the government's tax revenues', that 'Reducing tax revenues did not restrain government spending, at least not by enough to avoid the emergence of historically large deficits', and that 'Greater deficits did result in reduced private investment'. [[c-us8-reagan-friedman]]

pages.title: Ending the Cold War
pages.lede: The Reagan administration modernized American forces and in 1983 proposed missile defence; computed from BEA data, defence spending rose from about 6.4 percent of GDP in the third quarter of 1980 to about 7.9 percent in the third quarter of 1986. Reagan also negotiated: the INF Treaty of December 1987 eliminated 2,692 missiles, while the Iran-Contra affair led to 14 people being charged. Scholars disagree about how far American policy, material pressures or new ideas ended the Cold War.
body: The Reagan administration 'pursued a comprehensive modernization of U.S. nuclear and conventional forces.' [[c-us8-cw-buildup]] Computed from BEA data, national defense spending was about 6.4 percent of GDP in the third quarter of 1980, about 7.9 percent in the third quarter of 1986 and about 6.7 percent in the third quarter of 1991. [[c-us8-cw-defshare]] On 23 March 1983 Reagan proposed a missile defence aimed at 'rendering these nuclear weapons impotent and obsolete'; the Office of the Historian describes the Strategic Defense Initiative as a programme 'which Soviet leaders found highly threatening'. [[c-us8-cw-sdi]]

At Reykjavik in October 1986 Reagan and Gorbachev 'discussed the prospect of abolishing all nuclear weapons.' [[c-us8-cw-reykjavik]] At the Brandenburg Gate on 12 June 1987 Reagan said: 'General Secretary Gorbachev, if you seek peace, if you seek prosperity for the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, if you seek liberalization: Come here to this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, open this gate! Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!' [[c-us8-cw-berlin]] Peter Robinson, the speechwriter, writes that the State Department and the National Security Council 'submitted their own alternate drafts', and that 'In each, the call to tear down the wall was missing.' [[c-us8-cw-drafts]] The INF Treaty, signed on 8 December 1987, banned ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometres; it entered into force on 1 June 1988, and 'A total of 2,692 missiles was eliminated'. [[c-us8-cw-inf]] In Moscow in 1988 Reagan said that the term 'evil empire' belonged to 'another era.' [[c-us8-cw-era]]

In the Iran-Contra affair, in Britannica's description, the National Security Council 'became involved in secret weapons transactions and other activities that either were prohibited by the U.S. Congress or violated the stated public policy of the government.' The Boland Amendment of 1984 'banned direct or indirect U.S. military aid to the Contras'. On 13 November 1986 Reagan told the nation: 'We did not—repeat—did not trade weapons or anything else for hostages, nor will we.' On 4 March 1987 he said: 'A few months ago I told the American people I did not trade arms for hostages. My heart and my best intentions still tell me that's true, but the facts and the evidence tell me it is not.' [[c-us8-cw-irancontra]] Independent Counsel Walsh reported that '14 persons were charged'; 11 were convicted, 'two convictions were overturned on appeal', those of North and Poindexter, and President George H. W. Bush pardoned six people on 24 December 1992. [[c-us8-cw-walsh]] On presidential power and impeachment as doctrine, see US2.4.

Who ended the Cold War? Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1990 'for the leading role he played in the radical changes in East-West relations'. [[c-us8-cw-nobel]] Francis Sempa, asking whether Reagan was a crusader or a conciliator, answers: 'The answer, I believe, is that he was both'. In his account 'Reagan the crusader launched a political, military, psychological, and economic offensive designed to undermine Soviet power', while 'Reagan the conciliator engaged in summitry and arms control negotiations with a reform-oriented Mikhail Gorbachev'. He cites John Lewis Gaddis, who, Sempa writes, held that Reagan ended the Cold War by 'changing rather than containing' the Soviet Union. [[c-us8-cw-sempa]] Stephen Brooks and William Wohlforth argue, in the Belfer Center's summary of their article, that shifting material pressures 'had a much greater influence on Soviet foreign policy in the 1980s than previously thought.' [[c-us8-cw-bw]] Robert English, replying, faults them, in the same centre's summary, for privileging materialist explanations 'to the exclusion of other possible causes—in particular, the influence of "new thinkers" led by Mikhail Gorbachev'. [[c-us8-cw-english]] On the end of the Cold War worldwide, see 15.14 and 16.1.

pages.title: Bush and Clinton
pages.lede: In January 1991 Congress voted on the use of force against Iraq, 52 to 47 in the Senate and 250 to 183 in the House, and in November 1993 NAFTA passed the House with more Republican than Democratic votes. Republicans' Contract with America (1994), welfare reform (1996) and budget surpluses in fiscal 1998-2001 followed, and in December 1998 the House impeached Clinton on two articles, by 228 to 206 and 221 to 212, on which the Senate voted 45 to 55 and 50 to 50 in February 1999. Economists still disagree about NAFTA's effects and about welfare reform's results.
body: Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. A coalition 'Comprising forces from thirty-four countries' began the air war on 16 January 1991 and the ground war on 24 February, and the war ended on 28 February. [[c-us8-bc-gulf]] On 12 January 1991 the Senate passed a joint resolution to authorize the use of American forces under UN Security Council Resolution 678 by 52 to 47, Republicans voting 42 to 2 and Democrats 10 to 45; the House passed its resolution by 250 to 183, Democrats 86 to 179 and Republicans 164 to 3. [[c-us8-bc-gulfvotes]] The House passed NAFTA on 17 November 1993 by 234 to 200, Democrats 102 to 156 and Republicans 132 to 43, and the Senate on 20 November by 61 to 38. [[c-us8-bc-naftavotes]]

What did NAFTA do? Caliendo and Parro estimate that the 'U.S.'s welfare increases by 0.08%' and that trade within the bloc rose by 41 percent for the United States. [[c-us8-bc-nafta-gain]] Hakobyan and McLaren find NAFTA 'dramatically lowering wage growth for blue-collar workers in the most affected industries and localities'. [[c-us8-bc-nafta-loss]] The two findings measure different things: a small national average, and losses concentrated in particular places. On the China shock, see US8.12.

The Republicans' Contract with America was 'signed Sept. 27, 1994, on the Capitol steps'; among its pledges was to 'require all laws that apply to the rest of the country also apply equally to the Congress'. Apart from term limits, all its parts passed the House, and Newt Gingrich became 'the first Republican in 40 years to serve as speaker'. [[c-us8-bc-contract]] Welfare reform, which President Clinton signed as Public Law 104-193 on 22 August 1996, replaced AFDC with TANF, which now provides 'approximately $16.5 billion to states'. [[c-us8-bc-welfare]] Ron Haskins of Brookings, who had spent 14 years on the staff of the House Ways and Means Committee and wrote an inside history of the 1996 law, told Congress in 2006 that 'Between 1994 and 2005, the caseload declined about 60 percent' and that 'child poverty fell every year' from 1994 to 2000. [[c-us8-bc-haskins]] Shaefer and Edin find that the 'prevalence of extreme poverty has risen sharply since 1996, particularly among those most affected by the 1996 welfare reform.' [[c-us8-bc-shaefer]] Meyer, Wu, Mooers and Medalia, linking 2011 survey data to administrative records, reply that of the 3.6 million non-homeless households reporting cash income below $2 a person a day 'more than 90% are not in extreme poverty once we include in-kind transfers, replace survey reports of earnings and transfer receipt with administrative records, and account for the ownership of substantial assets', and conclude that extreme poverty 'cannot be substantially higher now due to welfare reform'. [[c-us8-bc-meyer]]

The federal budget, in deficit by 4.45 percent of GDP in fiscal 1992 and 0.26 percent in 1997, ran surpluses of 0.76 percent in 1998, 1.30 in 1999, 2.30 in 2000 and 1.21 in 2001, before returning to deficit in 2002. [[c-us8-bc-surplus]] The top income-tax rate rose to 31 percent in 1991, under President George H. W. Bush, and to 39.6 percent under the 1993 budget act. [[c-us8-reagan-rates]] The Treasury estimated that the 1990 budget act raised revenue by 0.41 percent of GDP in its year of enactment and by about 0.5 percent a year on average, and that the 1993 act raised it by 0.36 percent in its year of enactment and by about 0.6 percent a year on average. [[c-us8-reagan-scores]] On 19 December 1998 the House adopted two of four articles of impeachment against Clinton: the first by 228 to 206 (Republicans 223 to 5, Democrats 5 to 200) and the third by 221 to 212 (Republicans 216 to 12, Democrats 5 to 199); the second and fourth failed. [[c-us8-bc-houseimp]] At the Senate trial, on 12 February 1999, the Senate voted 45 to 55 on Article I (perjury), all 45 guilty votes being Republican, and 50 to 50 on Article II (obstruction), with five Republicans voting not guilty. [[c-us8-bc-impeach]] On impeachment as doctrine and the two-thirds rule, see US2.4.

pages.title: A changing people
pages.lede: Under IRCA (1986) nearly 2.7 million people became lawful permanent residents, and the Immigration Act of 1990 raised employment visas from 54,000 to 140,000 a year. Between the 2010 and 2020 censuses the Hispanic population grew 23 percent and the Asian-alone population 35.5 percent; estimates of the unauthorized population run from DHS's 11 million (January 2022) to Pew's 14 million (2023). USCIS still processes DACA renewals, though with a growing backlog, and official and independent counts of departures since January 2025 differ widely.
body: Reagan signed the Immigration Reform and Control Act on 6 November 1986, writing: 'The employer sanctions program is the keystone and major element.' Applicants for legalization had to show 'that they entered the United States before January 1, 1982', farmworkers had a separate route, and employers who hired unauthorized workers faced 'civil penalties of $250 to $10,000'. [[c-us8-imm-irca]] In the figures of DHS's Office of Immigration Statistics, nearly 2.7 million people became lawful permanent residents under IRCA: about 1.6 million who had lived in the country since before 1982 and 1.1 million special agricultural workers. [[c-us8-imm-irca27]] Signing the Immigration Act of 1990, George H. W. Bush said: 'This bill is good for families, good for business, good for crime fighting, and good for America.' The act set 'a flexible cap of 700,000 until 1995 and 675,000 thereafter', created 40,000 diversity visas, raised employment visas from 54,000 to 140,000 and created Temporary Protected Status. [[c-us8-imm-1990]]

Between the 2010 and 2020 censuses the Hispanic population grew 23 percent, from 50.5 million to 62.1 million (18.7 percent of the whole); the Asian-alone population grew 35.5 percent, to 19.9 million, and the White-alone population fell 8.6 percent. The Census Bureau warns that comparisons of the 2020 and 2010 race data 'should be made with caution', and that differences in the overall racial distributions are 'largely due to improvements in the design of the two separate questions for race data collection and processing as well as some demographic changes over the past 10 years.' [[c-us8-imm-census]] Population growth 'slowed to 0.5%' between July 2024 and July 2025 as net international migration declined, [[c-us8-imm-slow]] and the Congressional Budget Office 'reduced its projections of net immigration from 2025 to 2029'. [[c-us8-imm-cbo]] Estimates of the unauthorized population differ by source and date. DHS's statistics office estimated 11 million on 1 January 2022, as USAFacts reports it; [[c-us8-imm-dhs]] the Migration Policy Institute estimates 13.7 million as of mid-2023; [[c-us8-imm-mpi]] and Pew estimates 14 million in 2023, above its 2007 high of 12.2 million, with a likely fall of up to 1 million in the first half of 2025. [[c-us8-imm-pew]] Economists disagree about effects on wages: studying the 1980 Mariel boatlift, George Borjas finds that the wage of high-school dropouts in Miami 'dropped dramatically, by 10 to 30 percent', while Giovanni Peri and Vasil Yasenov, using 'a sample of non-Cuban high-school dropouts', 'find no significant difference in the wages of workers in Miami relative to its control after 1980.' [[c-us8-imm-mariel]]

DACA, announced on 15 June 2012, covered people 'under the age of 31 as of June 15, 2012' who had come before their 16th birthday and 'continuously resided in the United States since June 15, 2007'. [[c-us8-imm-daca]] On 17 January 2025 the Fifth Circuit largely affirmed a ruling that DACA was unlawful but 'narrowed the ruling to apply only to Texas'. CBS News reported that more than 525,000 people were enrolled at the end of June 2025, nearly 88,000 of them in Texas, and that under the administration's plan Texas residents would get deportation deferrals but not work authorization. [[c-us8-imm-dacacourt]] As consulted on 4 November 2026, USCIS was processing renewals and accepting, but not processing, initial requests; the latest reports found for this book, from the Texas Tribune (October 2025) and FWD.us (May 2026), describe Judge Hanen's implementing directions as still awaited. [[c-us8-imm-dacanow]] CBS News reported on 8 October 2026, citing federal data, that active DACA holders had fallen 14 percent, to 436,350, between September 2025 and 30 June 2026, while the backlog of pending renewal applications had more than quadrupled, to over 125,000. [[c-us8-imm-dacabacklog]]

Enforcement figures for 2025-26 come from different counters. ICE's budget document, as the Washington Times reported in April 2026, gave 442,637 removals in fiscal 2025 (Newsweek reported the same figure) and a target of '1,000,000 returns and removals' a year. [[c-us8-imm-ice]] DHS said, as Fox News reported in May 2026, that more than 3 million people had left, 'including an estimated 2.2 million "self-deportations"'. [[c-us8-imm-dhsclaim]] A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek in October 2026 that nearly 1.1 million had been deported as of September. [[c-us8-imm-dhsoct]] Marc Rosenblum of the Migration Policy Institute counts 'about 980,000' deportations from 20 January 2025 to 31 July 2026, 'a figure in line with the department's public statements'. He estimates between 1.3 million and 2.4 million total departures, deportations and self-departures together, of which 790,000 to 1.9 million were of immigrants with at least a year's residence. He judges it 'highly unlikely that 3 million immigrants have departed'. [[c-us8-imm-mpideport]] AP reported that the administration's own count was 1.2 million deported or removed, and wrote that 'The discrepancy could not immediately be reconciled.' White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said: 'President Trump has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history.' [[c-us8-imm-ap]] TRAC counted 65,765 people in ICE detention on 11 July 2026, 70.6 percent of them with no criminal conviction; [[c-us8-imm-trac]] ICE, as ABC News reported on 21 July 2026, said that 60 percent of them had a criminal record. [[c-us8-imm-abc]] On the second term's immigration policy, see US8.11.

pages.title: 9/11 at home
pages.sub: The AUMF, the Patriot Act, Homeland Security, Iraq and Guantánamo
pages.lede: The attacks of 11 September 2001 killed 2,977 people. Within weeks Congress authorised force against those responsible, 98 to 0 in the Senate and 420 to 1 in the House, and passed the USA PATRIOT Act; a Department of Homeland Security opened in 2003, and in October 2002 Congress authorised force against Iraq. Estimates of what the wars cost depend on what is counted, and in September 2026 fifteen wartime detainees remained at Guantánamo.
body: The attacks of 11 September 2001 'killed 2,977 people from 90 nations': 2,753 in New York, 184 at the Pentagon and 40 on Flight 93. [[c-us8-911-deaths]] For the attackers and the wars abroad, see 16.3. Congress passed an Authorization for Use of Military Force (AUMF), approved on 18 September. Its operative clause reads: 'That the President is authorized to use all necessary and appropriate force against those nations, organizations, or persons he determines planned, authorized, committed, or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001, or harbored such organizations or persons, in order to prevent any future acts of international terrorism against the United States by such nations, organizations or persons.' [[c-us8-911-aumf]] The Senate passed it 98 to 0 on 14 September, and the House 420 to 1, Republicans 214 to 0 and Democrats 204 to 1, the one vote against cast by Lee, a California Democrat. [[c-us8-911-aumfvote]] The text leaves it to the President to determine who 'planned, authorized, committed, or aided' the attacks; on presidential power as doctrine, see US2.4. [[c-us8-911-aumf]]

The USA PATRIOT Act passed the House 357 to 66 on 24 October 2001, Republicans 211 to 3 and Democrats 145 to 62, and the Senate 98 to 1 the next day, Feingold, a Wisconsin Democrat, casting the one vote against. [[c-us8-911-patriotvote]] Approved on 26 October, it included a Title II headed 'ENHANCED SURVEILLANCE PROCEDURES', and its section 215 dealt with 'ACCESS TO RECORDS AND OTHER ITEMS UNDER THE FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE SURVEILLANCE ACT.' [[c-us8-911-patriot]] After Congress passed the Homeland Security Act in November 2002, the new Department of Homeland Security combined 'all or part of 22 different federal departments and agencies', opening its doors on 1 March 2003. [[c-us8-911-dhs]]

In October 2002 Congress authorised force against Iraq. The resolution, approved on 16 October, provides: 'The President is authorized to use the Armed Forces of the United States as he determines to be necessary and appropriate in order to-- (1) defend the national security of the United States against the continuing threat posed by Iraq; and (2) enforce all relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions regarding Iraq.' [[c-us8-911-iraq]] The House passed it 296 to 133 on 10 October, Republicans 215 to 6 and Democrats 81 to 126; the Senate passed it 77 to 23 the next day, Republicans 48 to 1 and Democrats 29 to 21. Most House Democrats voted no, and most Senate Democrats yes. [[c-us8-911-iraqvote]] For the war itself and the dispute over the prewar intelligence, see 16.3. What the wars cost depends on what is counted. The Congressional Research Service counted $1.6 trillion appropriated for war operations through fiscal 2014, $815 billion for Iraq and $686 billion for Afghanistan and other counterterrorism operations. [[c-us8-911-crs]] Neta C. Crawford of Boston University, a co-director of the Costs of War project at Brown University's Watson Institute, estimates 'about $8 trillion in current dollars': $5.8 trillion spent from fiscal 2001 to 2022, counting interest on war borrowing, increases in the base defence budget, homeland security and veterans' care as well as $2.1 trillion in the Defense Department's overseas contingency appropriations, plus about $2.2 trillion in veterans' care owed to 2050. [[c-us8-911-cow]]

The prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, opened on 11 January 2002 with the arrival of 20 detainees. The military has held about 780 men and boys there; fifteen wartime prisoners remained in January 2026 and were still there in September. [[c-us8-911-gitmo]] In 2025 the base also held migrants, about 775 of them 'for days or weeks', and 54 men as of 9 January 2026. [[c-us8-911-migrants]] The case against Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three co-defendants, Walid bin Attash, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali and Mustafa al-Hawsawi, goes on. On 11 July 2025 the D.C. Circuit voted 2 to 1 to throw out plea deals that would have given Mohammed and two of them life sentences without parole, and on 19 October 2026 the Supreme Court declined to review former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin's decision to cancel the deals, Justice Kavanaugh recusing himself. [[c-us8-911-ksm]] In August 2026 a military judge set the trial to begin on 5 June 2028. Steve Vladeck of Georgetown University Law Center, a CNN legal analyst who had filed a brief urging the justices to take up the appeals, said that 'even the current summer 2028 trial date is entirely unrealistic' (CNN, republished by Scripps News). [[c-us8-911-trial]]

pages.title: The Great Recession at home
pages.sub: 2007 to 2012: TARP, the stimulus and Dodd-Frank
pages.lede: The recession that began in December 2007 lasted until June 2009; real GDP fell 4.3 percent, and unemployment peaked at 10 percent in October 2009. The House rejected the bank rescue, TARP, once and then passed it; the 2009 stimulus passed with three Republican votes, all in the Senate, and Dodd-Frank followed in 2010. Economists still differ over how much the rescue and the stimulus achieved.
body: The Great Recession 'began in December 2007 and ended in June 2009, which makes it the longest recession since World War II.' Real GDP 'fell 4.3 percent from its peak in 2007Q4 to its trough in 2009Q2'; home prices fell about 30 percent on average from their mid-2006 peak to mid-2009; the net worth of households and nonprofit organisations fell from about $69 trillion in 2007 to $55 trillion in 2009; and the unemployment rate 'peaked at 10 percent in October 2009'. [[c-us8-gr-recession]] In September 2008 Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy with 'a reported $639 billion in assets', the largest bankruptcy in American history at that time. [[c-us8-gr-lehman]] For the crisis worldwide, see 16.4. Annual unemployment rose from 4.6 percent in 2007 to 9.6 percent in 2010 and was still 8.1 percent in 2012 (chart). [[c-us8-gr-unemp]] RealtyTrac, counting properties with any foreclosure filing rather than completed foreclosures, found 2,824,674 such properties in 2009, 'a 120 percent increase' on 2007; in 2010 'A record 2.9 million properties received foreclosure filings.' [[c-us8-gr-foreclose]]

On 29 September 2008 the House rejected the bill carrying the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP), 205 to 228: Democrats voted 140 to 95 for it and Republicans 65 to 133 against. The Senate passed a revised bill 74 to 25 on 1 October, Democrats 39 to 9 and Republicans 34 to 15, and on 3 October the House passed it 263 to 171, Democrats 172 to 63 and Republicans 91 to 108. [[c-us8-gr-tarpvote]] In its final report, in April 2024, the Congressional Budget Office found that '$444 billion of the $700 billion initially authorized was disbursed' and that 'the government's total subsidy cost was $31 billion'; mortgage programmes cost about $31 billion and aid to the auto industry about $12 billion, while purchases of bank capital gained about $9 billion and investment partnerships for securitization markets about $3 billion. [[c-us8-gr-tarpcost]] Pietro Veronesi and Luigi Zingales estimate that the intervention of October 2008 'increased the value of banks' financial claims by $130 billion' at 'a taxpayers' cost of $21-$44 billion', and also conclude: 'The big winners of the plan were the bondholders of the three former investment banks and Citigroup, while the losers were JP Morgan shareholders and the US taxpayers.' [[c-us8-gr-vz]]

The stimulus, the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, passed both houses on 13 February 2009: the House by 246 to 183, with Democrats 246 to 7 and Republicans 0 to 176, and the Senate by 60 to 38, with three Republicans, Collins, Snowe and Specter, voting yes. [[c-us8-gr-arravote]] The Congressional Budget Office later put its total budgetary impact over 2009-2019 at 'nearly $840 billion' and estimated that its effects on output 'peaked in the first half of 2010.' [[c-us8-gr-arracbo]] Dodd-Frank passed the House 237 to 192 on 30 June 2010, Democrats 234 to 19 and Republicans 3 to 173, and the Senate 60 to 39 on 15 July, with three Republicans (Brown, Collins and Snowe) voting yes and one Democrat (Feingold) voting no. [[c-us8-gr-dfvote]]

How much did the stimulus do? Before it passed, Christina Romer of the Council of Economic Advisers and Jared Bernstein of the Vice-President's office estimated that a package of about $775 billion 'is expected to create between three and four million jobs by the end of 2010', while warning that such estimates 'are subject to significant margins of error.' [[c-us8-gr-romer]] John B. Taylor, studying the stimulus packages of the 2000s, found that they 'had little if any direct impact on consumption or government purchases' and that 'Households largely saved the transfers and tax rebates.' [[c-us8-gr-taylor]] Gabriel Chodorow-Reich, reviewing evidence from differences between places, puts the cross-sectional spending multiplier at about 1.8 and concludes that the evidence points to 'a national no-monetary-policy-response multiplier of 1.7 or above.' [[c-us8-gr-cr]] In a 2014 survey of the Clark Center's IGM panel, 36 economists agreed or strongly agreed and 1 disagreed that the act had lowered unemployment at the end of 2010; on whether its benefits would exceed its costs, 25 agreed, 10 were uncertain and 2 disagreed. [[c-us8-gr-igm]]

pages.title: Obama
pages.sub: 2008 to 2016: the ACA, the midterms and Obergefell
pages.lede: Barack Obama won the 2008 election with 52.93 percent of the popular vote and 365 electoral votes, and was re-elected in 2012 with 51.06 percent and 332. The Affordable Care Act passed in 2009-10 without a Republican vote, and the share of Americans without health insurance fell; Republicans won the House in 2010 and enlarged their majority in 2014. In Obergefell v. Hodges (2015) the Supreme Court held, 5 to 4, that same-sex couples may exercise the fundamental right to marry, and in November 2025 it declined to hear a petition asking it to overrule that decision.
body: In 2008, by the Federal Election Commission's count, Barack Obama won 69,498,516 votes (52.93 percent) and 365 electoral votes, and John McCain 59,948,323 (45.65 percent) and 173. [[c-us8-obama-elec]] The Affordable Care Act (H.R. 3590) passed the Senate 60 to 39 on 24 December 2009, every Republican present voting no; on 21 March 2010 the House concurred 219 to 212, Democrats 219 to 34 and Republicans 0 to 178. [[c-us8-obama-acavote]] The Congressional Budget Office and the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated that the law and its companion reconciliation act together 'would produce a net reduction in federal deficits of $143 billion over the 2010–2019 period'. [[c-us8-obama-acacbo]]

By the Census Bureau's Current Population Survey, 13.3 percent of Americans, 41.8 million people, lacked health insurance in 2013, 10.4 percent in 2014 and 8.8 percent, 28.1 million, in 2016; in 2024, 92.0 percent had coverage (chart). [[c-us8-obama-census]] The CDC's National Health Interview Survey, which counts people uninsured at the time of interview, gives 9.7 percent in 2020, 7.6 percent in 2023, 8.2 percent in 2024 and 8.3 percent, 28.0 million people, in 2025. [[c-us8-obama-nhis]] Studies of the law's effects ask different questions. Sarah Miller, Norman Johnson and Laura Wherry, comparing near-elderly adults 'most likely to benefit', identified by socioeconomic status, in states that expanded Medicaid under the ACA and in states that did not, find that mortality had 'trended similarly' before the expansions and that afterwards those in expansion states 'experienced a 0.132 percentage point decline in annual mortality, a 9.4 percent reduction over the sample mean'. [[c-us8-obama-mjw]] In 2014 the Congressional Budget Office projected that the law would reduce hours worked 'by about 1.5 percent to 2.0 percent' from 2017 to 2024, equal to about 2.0 million full-time-equivalent workers in 2017 and 2.5 million in 2024, 'almost entirely because workers will choose to supply less labor.' [[c-us8-obama-cbo]]

Theda Skocpol and Vanessa Williamson, as their book on the Tea Party (2011) is summarised on a page of Harvard's Weatherhead Center, describe the movement as joining grassroots activists with national elites and funders, who used grassroots energy to further long-standing goals. [[c-us8-obama-tp]] The organisation Tea Party Patriots names, on its current website, 'our three core values of fiscal responsibility, constitutionally limited government, and free markets.' [[c-us8-obama-tpp]] At the start of the 111th Congress Democrats held 257 House seats and Republicans 178; at the start of the 112th, after the 2010 midterm, Republicans held 242 and Democrats 193. After the 2014 midterm Republicans held 247 seats to the Democrats' 188. [[c-us8-obama-house]] In 2012 Obama was re-elected with 65,915,795 votes (51.06 percent) and 332 electoral votes to Mitt Romney's 60,933,504 (47.20 percent) and 206. [[c-us8-obama-elec2012]] Unemployment was 7.8 percent in January 2009, peaked at 10.0 percent in October 2009 and was 4.7 percent in January 2017 (BLS). [[c-us8-obama-jobs]] On parties and polarisation, see US2.14 and US8.13.

On 26 June 2015, in Obergefell v. Hodges, the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4. Justice Kennedy wrote for the Court: 'The Court now holds that same-sex couples may exercise the fundamental right to marry', and added that there is 'no lawful basis for a State to refuse to recognize a lawful same-sex marriage performed in another State'. Of the petitioners he wrote: 'They ask for equal dignity in the eyes of the law.' [[c-us8-obama-oberg]] Chief Justice Roberts, joined by Justices Scalia and Thomas, wrote the lead dissent, and Scalia, Thomas and Alito each wrote one too. Roberts wrote: 'But this Court is not a legislature. Whether same-sex marriage is a good idea should be of no concern to us.' And: 'Under the Constitution, judges have power to say what the law is, not what it should be.' [[c-us8-obama-dissent]] On 10 November 2025 the Court denied Kim Davis's petition asking it to overrule Obergefell, with no noted dissent. [[c-us8-obama-davis]]

pages.title: Trump's first term
pages.lede: Donald Trump won the presidency in 2016 with 304 electoral votes, while Hillary Clinton led the popular vote by 2,868,686. His first term brought the 2017 tax law, a 25 percent tariff on steel and a Section 301 case against China, 226 or 234 new federal judges depending on the count, and two impeachments that ended in acquittal; Democrats won the House in the 2018 midterm. In 2020 the CDC counted 350,831 deaths with COVID-19 as the underlying cause, the first COVID-19 vaccine was authorised for emergency use in December, and Joe Biden won the election by 306 electoral votes to 232.
body: In 2016, by the Federal Election Commission's count, Hillary Clinton won 65,853,514 votes (48.18 percent) and Donald Trump 62,984,828 (46.09 percent), a margin of 2,868,686 for Clinton; the electors cast 304 votes for Trump and 227 for Clinton. Seven electors voted for others, among them two in Texas, one for John Kasich and one for Ron Paul. [[c-us8-t1-elec2016]] The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act passed the Senate 51 to 48 in the early hours of 20 December 2017, every Republican present voting yes and no Democrat or independent doing so, and the House 224 to 201 later that day, Republicans 224 to 12 and Democrats 0 to 189. [[c-us8-t1-tcja]] The Congressional Budget Office and the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated that it would 'increase the deficit by $1,455 billion over the next 10 years, excluding effects from macroeconomic feedback'; in September 2025 CBO found its estimates 'consistent with observed outcomes in 2018 and 2019'. [[c-us8-t1-tcjacbo]] Gabriel Chodorow-Reich, Matthew Smith, Owen Zidar and Eric Zwick (2024) find that domestic investment by firms with the average tax change rose '20% versus a no-change baseline', but that for the corporate provisions the revenue feedback from growth 'offsets only 2p.p. of the direct cost of 41% of pre-TCJA corporate revenue'. [[c-us8-t1-tcjainv]]

Proclamation 9705 of 8 March 2018 imposed 'a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on steel articles'. [[c-us8-t1-steel]] On 22 March 2018 the U.S. Trade Representative found under Section 301 that China's technology-transfer practices were 'unreasonable and burdens or restricts U.S. commerce'. [[c-us8-t1-china]] Economists have measured the tariffs' effects. Amiti, Redding and Weinstein (2019) find that 'the full incidence of the tariffs has fallen on domestic consumers and importers so far'. [[c-us8-t1-ard]] Autor, Beck, Dorn and Hanson (2024) find that 'The trade-war has not to date provided economic help to the US heartland', and also that exposed regions 'became less likely to identify as Democrats'. [[c-us8-t1-adbh]] The U.S. International Trade Commission (2023) found that the Section 232 tariffs 'increased U.S. production of steel products by 1.9 percent', while the steel and aluminum tariffs together 'decreased production in downstream industries 0.6 percent on average'; Michael Stumo of the Coalition for a Prosperous America, an advocacy group that says it represents 'domestic producers and workers', said that 'tariffs are a critical reshoring tool to stimulate domestic production'. [[c-us8-t1-usitc]] On tariffs and the courts in 2025-26, see US2.13; on trade with China, see US8.12. Pew Research Center counts 226 judges appointed in Trump's single term, against 320 for Obama and 322 for George W. Bush over two terms each, including 3 Supreme Court justices and 54 appellate judges, 'one short of the 55 Obama appointed'. Pew counts only the Supreme Court, the appeals courts and the district courts; Ballotpedia counts '234 Article III federal judges through December 31, 2020', among them 174 district judges, and includes the Court of International Trade, which Pew leaves out; neither source reconciles the two totals. [[c-us8-t1-judges]]

In the 2018 midterm Democrats won the House: at the start of the 116th Congress they held 235 seats to the Republicans' 199, with one seat vacant, against 194 to 241 two years earlier. [[c-us8-t1-house]] On 18 December 2019 the House impeached Trump: Article I (abuse of power) passed 230 to 197, with no Republican voting yes and Democrats 229 to 2, and Article II (obstruction of Congress) 229 to 198. [[c-us8-t1-imp1]] On 5 February 2020 the Senate acquitted him, 48 to 52 on Article I, Romney the only Republican voting guilty, and 47 to 53 on Article II. [[c-us8-t1-acq1]] After the events of 6 January 2021 (US8.9) the House impeached him again on 13 January, on an article headed 'incitement of insurrection', 232 to 197, with 10 Republicans voting yes. On 13 February the Senate voted 57 to 43 to convict, short of the two-thirds required; the seven Republicans voting guilty were Burr, Cassidy, Collins, Murkowski, Romney, Sasse and Toomey. [[c-us8-t1-imp2]] For impeachment as doctrine, see US2.4.

Unemployment, 4.7 percent in January 2017, was 3.5 percent in February 2020, rose to 14.8 percent in April 2020 and was 6.4 percent in January 2021; real GDP grew 2.5 percent in 2017, 3.0 in 2018 and 2.6 in 2019 and fell 2.1 percent in 2020 (BLS; BEA, current estimates). [[c-us8-t1-jobs]] The CARES Act passed the Senate 96 to 0 on 25 March 2020 and was signed into law on 27 March; the Congressional Budget Office and the Joint Committee on Taxation estimated that it would 'increase federal deficits by about $1.7 trillion over the 2020-2030 period'. [[c-us8-t1-cares]] On 11 December 2020 the Food and Drug Administration issued the first emergency use authorization for a COVID-19 vaccine. [[c-us8-t1-vax]] The CDC counted 350,831 deaths in 2020 with COVID-19 as the underlying cause; counting it as underlying or contributing cause, the toll was 384,536 in 2020 and, provisionally, 460,513 in 2021. [[c-us8-t1-covid]] For the pandemic worldwide, see 16.11. In the 2020 election Joe Biden won 81,283,501 votes (51.31 percent) to Trump's 74,223,975 (46.85 percent), a margin of 7,059,526, and 306 electoral votes to 232. [[c-us8-t1-elec2020]]

pages.title: January 6 and its aftermath
pages.lede: On 6 January 2021, when Congress was scheduled to count the electoral votes, rioters broke into the Capitol; a report of a bipartisan Senate investigation called it 'a violent and unprecedented attack on the U.S. Capitol', found that about 140 officers reported injuries and that seven people, three of them officers, 'ultimately lost their lives', and recorded that Congress affirmed the electoral result at 3:42 a.m. on 7 January. The Justice Department charged about 1,583 people, and on 20 January 2025 President Trump commuted 14 sentences and pardoned all others convicted. The two parties describe the day, the pardons and the investigations in their own and opposing terms, and polls in January 2025 found majorities against the pardons.
body: On 6 January 2021, in the words of the report of the Senate Homeland Security and Rules committees (released 8 June 2021), 'Members of Congress were scheduled to perform their constitutional obligation to count the electoral votes' (for the 2020 result, see US8.8). 'Most demonstrators headed to the Ellipse, near the White House, for the "Save America" rally'. 'At approximately 12:53 p.m.', the report records, individuals in a crowd at the Capitol 'picked up one of the metal bike racks'. 'Rioters, attempting to disrupt the Joint Session of Congress, broke into the Capitol building', and 'Vice President Pence and congressional leaders were evacuated to secure locations.' The D.C. National Guard 'began arriving at the Capitol Complex at 5:20 p.m.', 'more than four hours after the barriers at the Capitol were first breached.' Congress reconvened that evening, and 'the Joint Session of Congress officially affirmed the results of the Electoral College at 3:42 a.m. on January 7.' 'Approximately 140 law enforcement officers reported injuries suffered during the attack', and 'seven individuals, including three law enforcement officers, ultimately lost their lives.' The report, which called the day 'a violent and unprecedented attack on the U.S. Capitol', examined 'the security, planning, and response failures' behind it. [[c-us8-j6-senate]]

The House select committee on the January 6th attack issued its final report (H. Rept. 117-663) on 22 December 2022. It states that 'the central cause of January 6th was one man, former President Donald Trump, whom many others followed. None of the events of January 6th would have happened without him.' [[c-us8-j6-house]] The House had impeached Trump a second time on 13 January 2021, and the Senate's 57 votes to convict fell short of two-thirds (US8.8); on impeachment and presidential immunity as doctrine, see US2.4. [[c-us8-t1-imp2]] The U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Columbia reported that about 1,583 people had been federally charged 'with crimes associated with the attack of the U.S. Capitol', about 608 of them with 'assaulting resisting, or impeding law enforcement agents or officers'; about 1,100 had been sentenced, and 170 more had pleaded guilty or been found guilty and awaited sentencing. ABC News reported the charge figures on 6 January 2025. [[c-us8-j6-doj]]

On 20 January 2025 President Trump issued a proclamation that states: 'This proclamation ends a grave national injustice that has been perpetrated upon the American people over the last four years and begins a process of national reconciliation.' It commuted the sentences of fourteen named people 'to time served as of January 20, 2025'; granted 'a full, complete and unconditional pardon to all other individuals convicted of offenses related to events that occurred at or near the United States Capitol on January 6, 2021'; and directed the Attorney General to 'pursue dismissal with prejudice to the government of all pending indictments.' [[c-us8-j6-pardon]] In May 2025 the Justice Department agreed in principle to pay 'a little under $5 million' to the family of Ashli Babbitt, who was shot by a Capitol Police lieutenant. The Capitol Police chief, J. Thomas Manger, wrote to his officers that he 'completely disagree[d] with the Department of Justice's decision', adding: 'In 2021, the DOJ said that there was no evidence to show that law enforcement broke the law.' [[c-us8-j6-babbitt]] A Republican-led House subcommittee chaired by Barry Loudermilk is reinvestigating the attack. Its first hearing was titled 'Examining the Investigation into the DNC and RNC Pipe Bombs'. NPR, checking claims made at the hearing, noted that 'The president has direct control of the D.C. National Guard', and that a Justice Department inspector general had found no evidence 'showing or suggesting that the FBI had undercover employees in the various protest crowds, or at the Capitol, on January 6.' Brian Cole Jr., charged with placing the two pipe bombs, 'which never exploded', pleaded not guilty; a grand jury returned a new, eight-count indictment on 30 September 2026, and his trial, set in July, is scheduled for 16 February 2027. [[c-us8-j6-sub]]

Each side describes these events in its own words. On the fifth anniversary Loudermilk said: 'True accountability requires focusing on facts, not selective storytelling for partisan gain.' A December 2024 interim report by a House Administration subcommittee he chaired said that 'The January 6 Select Committee was improperly constituted and lacked authority.' [[c-us8-j6-cha]] A White House website blamed the Capitol Police for turning a 'peaceful demonstration into chaos.' Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, said: 'Donald Trump and far-right extremists in Congress have repeatedly attempted to rewrite history.' [[c-us8-j6-anniv]] On the pardons, Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, said on 21 January 2025: 'There is no other way to describe President Trump's pardon of Jan. 6 offenders than un-American.' [[c-us8-j6-schumer]] In a Marist poll of 7-9 January 2025, before the proclamation, 62 percent disapproved and 35 percent approved of pardoning people 'convicted of attacking the Capitol'; Republicans approved, 64 to 30 percent, and 89 percent of Democrats disapproved. In a Reuters/Ipsos poll of 20-21 January, 58 percent said Trump should not pardon all people convicted. Washington Post-University of Maryland polls, as reported by the Christian Science Monitor, found that the share saying punishments were 'not harsh enough' fell from more than half in 2021 to 38 percent in 2023, and that in December 2024 90 percent of Democrats and 40 percent of Republicans opposed pardons. [[c-us8-j6-polls]]

pages.title: Biden
pages.sub: Rescue, inflation and the 2024 election, 2021 to 2025
pages.lede: The American Rescue Plan passed in March 2021 with no Republican votes, and consumer prices rose 4.7 percent in 2021 and 8.0 percent in 2022; Bernanke and Blanchard trace most of the surge to price shocks, while San Francisco Fed economists estimate that fiscal support added about 3 points by the end of 2021. The infrastructure and CHIPS laws drew Republican votes in both chambers, while the Inflation Reduction Act passed on party lines. In the certified 2024 result Donald Trump won 312 electoral votes to Kamala Harris's 226.
body: The Senate passed the American Rescue Plan on 6 March 2021 by 50 votes to 49, with no Republican voting yes; the House agreed on 10 March by 220 to 211, Democrats voting 220-1 and Republicans 0-210. [[c-us8-biden-arp]] CBO estimated that the Senate-passed bill would add about $1.86 trillion to deficits over 2021-2030. [[c-us8-biden-arp-cbo]] For COVID-19 worldwide, see 16.11.

Consumer prices, which had risen 1.2 percent in 2020, rose 4.7 percent in 2021, 8.0 percent in 2022, 4.1 percent in 2023 and 2.9 percent in 2024, on the BLS CPI-U annual averages. [[c-us8-biden-cpi]] Over the twelve months to June 2022 they rose 9.1 percent, which the BLS called 'the largest 12-month increase since the period ending November 1981'; over the twelve months to December 2024 the rise was 2.9 percent. [[c-us8-biden-peak]] Unemployment, 6.4 percent in January 2021, fell to 3.4 percent in April 2023 and was 4.0 percent in January 2025; real GDP grew 6.3 percent in 2021, 2.4 percent in 2022, 2.9 percent in 2023 and 3.0 percent in 2024 (BEA, current estimates). [[c-us8-biden-jobs]]

Economists differ on the causes. Ben Bernanke and Olivier Blanchard (2025) conclude that, 'contrary to early concerns that inflation would be spurred by overheated labor markets, most of the inflation surge resulted from shocks to prices given wages', though they add that tight labor markets have had a more persistent effect on wages and inflation. [[c-us8-biden-bb]] Economists at the San Francisco Fed, comparing the United States with other rich countries in March 2022, estimated that American fiscal support 'may have contributed to this divergence by raising inflation about 3 percentage points by the end of 2021', while warning that the estimate carried 'considerable uncertainty' and placing it in the upper range of other research. [[c-us8-biden-frbsf]] The two findings measure different things and need not conflict.

The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act passed the Senate 69-30 in August 2021, with 19 Republicans in favour, and the House 228-206 in November, with 13 Republicans voting yes and 6 Democrats no. [[c-us8-biden-iija]] NBC News reported CBO's estimate that it would add $256 billion to projected deficits over ten years. [[c-us8-biden-iija-cbo]] The CHIPS and Science bill passed in July 2022 with 17 Republican votes in the Senate and 24 in the House [[c-us8-biden-chips]], and CBO estimated that it would add $79 billion to deficits through 2031. [[c-us8-biden-chips-cbo]] The Inflation Reduction Act passed the Senate 51-50 on the Vice President's tie-breaking vote and the House 220-207, on party lines in both [[c-us8-biden-ira]]; CBO's estimate of the enacted law was a net deficit reduction of $58.1 billion over 2022-2031; under scorekeeping rules that figure leaves out an estimated $180 billion of added revenue from the law's IRS enforcement funding, which CBO reported separately. [[c-us8-biden-ira-cbo]]

On 26 August 2021 an ISIS-K bombing at Abbey Gate, Kabul, killed at least 160 Afghan civilians and 13 American service members. [[c-us8-biden-abbey]] On 31 August Biden said that 'more than 120,000 people' had been evacuated, spoke of 'The extraordinary success of this mission', and declared: 'I was not going to extend this forever war, and I was not extending a forever exit.' [[c-us8-biden-aug31]] The State Department's after-action review, released in June 2023, found that 'during both administrations' there was 'insufficient senior-level consideration of worst-case scenarios and how quickly those might follow'; it treated the decisions of both presidents to end the mission as beyond its scope, while saying they 'had serious consequences'. [[c-us8-biden-afg-review]] (The wars themselves are in 16.3.) In April 2024 the House passed aid for Ukraine 311-112, with Republicans splitting 101 to 112, and the Senate cleared the combined package 79-18 (see 16.5). [[c-us8-biden-ukraine]] In the certified 2024 result Trump received 77,302,580 votes (49.80 percent) and 312 electoral votes; Harris received 75,017,613 (48.32 percent) and 226. [[c-us8-biden-2024]]
