pages.title: Trump's second term
pages.lede: Trump signed 225 executive orders in 2025; in February 2026 the Supreme Court held 6-3 that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, and other trade statutes were used instead; economists and the administration dispute who bears the tariffs' cost. CBO estimated that the 2025 reconciliation act adds $3.4 trillion to deficits over ten years, which the White House's economists contest; Pew and GAO measured a federal workforce about a tenth smaller, and MPI's count of about 980,000 deportations stands beside DHS officials' claim of more than 3 million departures. In the third quarter of 2026 output grew at a 3.4 percent annual rate, unemployment was 4.2 percent and consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher than a year earlier; the midterm elections were held on 3 November 2026, and this book's status line is 'as of 2 November 2026'.
body: According to the Federal Register, President Trump signed 225 executive orders in 2025, numbered EO 14147 to EO 14371. [[c-us8-t2-eo]] The tariffs are told in depth in US2.13. In brief: on 20 February 2026, in Learning Resources v. Trump, the Supreme Court held 6-3 that 'IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs'; Justice Kavanaugh, joined by Thomas and Alito, dissented, arguing that text, history and precedent show that it does. [[c-us8-t2-learning]] The President then imposed a 10% surcharge under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows up to 15% for 150 days. It was collected from 24 February 2026; an increase to 15% that he announced on 21 February was never put into effect. The surcharge expired on 24 July 2026, a 2-1 trade-court ruling against it having been stayed on appeal. [[c-us8-t2-122]] That day Section 301 tariffs of 10% or 12.5% on imports from 60 trading partners took effect; as of 12 October 2026 a challenge had been argued but not decided. [[c-us8-t2-301]] CBO estimates that about $130 billion of IEEPA tariffs was refunded in fiscal 2026. [[c-us8-t2-refund]]

Economists differ on who pays. Mary Amiti and colleagues at the New York Fed found that 'nearly 90 percent of the tariffs' economic burden fell on U.S. firms and consumers' in 2025; the National Economic Council director, Kevin Hassett, called it 'the worst paper I've ever seen in the history of the Federal Reserve System', saying its authors were 'basically only looking at changes in prices'. [[c-us8-t2-tariff-burden]] Caroline Freund, as summarised by the Tax Foundation, estimates that 'foreigners have absorbed 47 percent of the tariff burden while US importers paid 53 percent'. [[c-us8-t2-tariff-freund]] The White House Council of Economic Advisers reported in July 2025 that tariffs 'have not reduced the disinflationary impulse from imported goods as of May', while noting that its analysis did not identify what prices would have done without tariffs. [[c-us8-t2-tariff-cea]] Looking ahead, the Yale Budget Lab estimated in July 2026 that current tariffs would raise consumer prices by about 0.7 percent, about $1,100 a household a year, and the Tax Foundation that they raise taxes by an average of $820 a household in 2026 and lower long-run GDP by 0.4 percent. [[c-us8-t2-tariff-cost]]

Immigration enforcement is treated in US8.4. The Migration Policy Institute counts about 980,000 deportations by ICE and CBP between 20 January 2025 and 31 July 2026; DHS officials have claimed more than 3 million total departures, including about 2 million self-departures, which MPI says is about double its own estimate. [[c-us8-t2-deport]] US8.4 also gives the administration's own count of deportations, as AP reported it.

On the civil service, Pew's analysis of OPM data found that the civilian federal workforce shrank by 10.3 percent in 2025, from 2,312,301 to 2,074,649. [[c-us8-t2-workforce]] GAO, covering 22 agencies to January 2026, found a fall of nearly 256,000, more than 11 percent, as agencies offered incentives to resign or retire, carried out reductions in force and restricted hiring. [[c-us8-t2-gao]] GAO also estimated, as OPM quoted it, that agencies spent about $9.5 billion on paid administrative leave in 2025, about $6.7 billion of it under the deferred resignation program; OPM replied that for 'a one-time expense of at most $9.5 billion, taxpayers save more than $40 billion each year', a figure it computed itself. [[c-us8-t2-leave]] The Partnership for Public Service, a good-government group, put their cost to the economy at 'more than $165.6 billion', mostly modelled from cancelled science grants and disengaged staff; its data director called it 'a conservative estimate'. [[c-us8-t2-pps]] In November 2025 the Washington Examiner reported that DOGE had closed eight months early. [[c-us8-t2-doge]]

CBO estimated on 21 July 2025 that the 2025 reconciliation act (Public Law 119-21) increases deficits by $3.4 trillion over 2025-2034, as revenues fall by $4.5 trillion and direct spending by $1.1 trillion. [[c-us8-t2-obbba]] The White House Council of Economic Advisers, assuming growth about 1.1 to 1.2 percent higher a year on average over the law's first four years, projected in June 2025 '$2.1 to $2.3 trillion in offsetting deficit reduction due to higher growth from the OBBB tax provisions', and the White House said that, counting projected growth, the bill meant 'deficit reduction of $755 billion relative to the CBO's tax hike baseline'. [[c-us8-t2-cea-obbba]] As reported by Georgetown's Center for Children and Families, CBO projected 10 million more uninsured people in 2034, 5.3 million of them from the Medicaid work requirement before interactions. [[c-us8-t2-uninsured]] Christopher Jacobs of The Federalist disputed one provision, which accounted for about 100,000 of that total: it 'didn't take anything away from anyone, or any state, now', he wrote, calling its supposed effect 'highly speculative'. He did not contest CBO's figures for the work requirement or the limits on immigrants' eligibility, and wrote that 'a community engagement requirement for program recipients seems reasonable.' [[c-us8-t2-jacobs]]

A 43-day shutdown, which CBS News called the longest in history, ended on 12 November 2025: Democrats had demanded an extension of the expiring Affordable Care Act tax credits, Republicans had insisted that health care be negotiated separately, and the deal promised a vote on the tax credits in December. [[c-us8-t2-shutdown]] On 11 December 2025 the Senate rejected both a Democratic three-year extension and a Republican alternative, each 51-48, short of the 60 votes needed; the House passed a three-year extension 230-196 on 8 January 2026, with 17 Republicans in favour; and KFF reported in October 2026 that the enhanced credits had expired in 2026. [[c-us8-t2-aca]]

The latest official data, each as of its release date: real GDP grew at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026, after 2.2 percent in the second (BEA advance estimate, 29 October) [[c-us8-t2-gdp]]; payrolls rose by 29,000 in September and unemployment was 4.2 percent (BLS, 2 October) [[c-us8-t2-jobs]]; and consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher than a year earlier, 2.6 percent excluding food and energy (BLS, 14 October). [[c-us8-t2-cpi]] For 2025 as a whole the CPI-U annual average rose 2.6 percent. [[c-us8-biden-cpi]] The midterm elections, for all 435 House seats among other offices, were held on 3 November 2026; this book reports no results. [[c-us8-t2-midterms]]

pages.title: The economy since 1980
pages.lede: Piketty, Saez and Zucman find that the bottom half's pretax income stagnated while top incomes boomed; Auten and Splinter, adjusting tax data differently, find top shares lower and after-tax top shares little changed. Economists likewise differ on whether pay has kept up with productivity and on how many manufacturing jobs Chinese imports cost. Manufacturing employment fell from about 19.6 million in June 1979 to about 12.7 million in September 2026, and union membership from 20.1 percent of wage and salary workers in 1983 to 10.0 percent in 2025.
body: How far inequality has risen depends on how income is measured. Thomas Piketty, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman (2018), combining tax, survey and national-accounts data, find that pretax income 'has stagnated for the bottom 50% of the distribution at about $16,000 a year', while 'Income has boomed at the top.' [[c-us8-econ-psz]] Gerald Auten and David Splinter (2024) argue that estimates built only on tax returns 'are biased by tax-base changes', 'social changes, and missing income sources'. Adjusting for these, they find top shares 'lower' and rising 'less since 1980 than other studies using tax data', with 'little change in aftertax top income shares', and conclude that 'increasing government transfers and tax progressivity have resulted in rising real incomes for all income groups.' [[c-us8-econ-as]]

A second debate concerns pay. The Economic Policy Institute reports that from 1979 to 2020 net productivity rose 61.8 percent while the hourly pay of typical workers, production and nonsupervisory employees, rose 17.5 percent. [[c-us8-econ-epi]] Martin Feldstein (2008) found that 'total compensation per hour' rose at about the same rate as productivity from 1970 to 2006, once both are adjusted for prices in the same way. [[c-us8-econ-feldstein]] Anna Stansbury and Lawrence Summers (2017) take a middle position: a point of extra productivity growth has gone with 0.7 to 1 point of extra median compensation growth, but 'other factors orthogonal to productivity have been acting to suppress typical compensation'. [[c-us8-econ-ss]]

On trade, David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson (2013) find that, between 1990 and 2007, Chinese 'import competition explains one-quarter of the contemporaneous aggregate decline in US manufacturing employment', and in 2021 that its effects 'are present out to 2019'. [[c-us8-econ-adh]] Lorenzo Caliendo, Maximiliano Dvorkin and Fernando Parro (2019), modelling the whole economy, estimate a loss of about 0.55 million manufacturing jobs, about 16 percent of the decline from 2000 to 2007, and find that 'The U.S. gains in the aggregate'. [[c-us8-econ-cdp]] Nicholas Bloom and colleagues (2019) find the losses concentrated in 'large, importing firms that simultaneously expand employment in non-manufacturing.' [[c-us8-econ-bloom]] For China's rise, see 16.2.

Manufacturing employment reached its all-time peak, 19.6 million, in June 1979, according to the BLS. In the BLS series it was about 17.3 million in January 2000, 11.4 million in February 2010 and 12.7 million in September 2026. [[c-us8-econ-mfg]] Union membership fell from 20.1 percent of wage and salary workers (17.7 million) in 1983 to 10.0 percent (14.7 million) in 2025, when the public-sector rate was 32.9 percent and the private-sector rate 5.9 percent. [[c-us8-econ-union]] National health spending grew 7.2 percent in 2024 to $5.3 trillion, or $15,474 a person and 18.0 percent of GDP. [[c-us8-econ-health]]

practice.q: Why do Auten and Splinter find a smaller rise in top income shares than Piketty, Saez and Zucman?
choices: They adjust tax-return data for tax-base changes and missing income
They study a different country, where top incomes rose more slowly
They find that after-tax top income shares rose sharply after 1980
They leave government transfers out of their measures of household income
practice.why: Auten and Splinter argue that tax-return estimates are biased by tax-base changes, social changes and missing income sources; their adjustments lower the measured rise. Piketty, Saez and Zucman combine tax, survey and national-accounts data and find income booming at the top.

wrong.1: Both teams study the United States.
wrong.2: They find 'little change in aftertax top income shares'.
wrong.3: They conclude that rising government transfers and tax progressivity have raised real incomes for all income groups.

practice.q: Caliendo, Dvorkin and Parro estimate a smaller manufacturing job loss from Chinese imports than Autor, Dorn and Hanson. What best explains the difference?
choices: They model the whole economy rather than comparing local labor markets
They find that trade with China created manufacturing jobs on net
They study the 2010s, after the worst of the China shock had already passed
They count service jobs, which offset most manufacturing losses
practice.why: The method changes the answer: a general-equilibrium model of the whole economy finds about 0.55 million jobs lost and aggregate gains for the United States, where Autor, Dorn and Hanson compare more- and less-exposed local markets. The two also cover different periods (1990-2007 and 2000-2007).

wrong.1: They estimate a loss of about 0.55 million manufacturing jobs.
wrong.2: Their figure is about 16 percent of the decline in manufacturing employment from 2000 to 2007.
wrong.3: Their headline estimate is of manufacturing jobs.

pages.title: Faith and polarization
pages.lede: The share of Americans with consistently liberal or conservative views doubled in the two decades to 2014, and by 2022 most Republicans and most Democrats called members of the other party more immoral than other Americans. Pew's 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study found 62 percent of adults Christian, down from 78 percent in 2007, and 29 percent unaffiliated, a rise that has levelled off, at least for now. Anti-Jewish incidents made up most religion-based hate crimes in the FBI figures for 2024 and 2025, as reported by the ADL, and Gallup's average confidence in institutions stood at 27 percent in 2026.
body: Pew found in 2014 that the share of Americans holding consistently liberal or consistently conservative views 'has doubled over the past two decades from 10% to 21%.' [[c-us8-faith-pew2014]] In 2022, 72 percent of Republicans said Democrats were more immoral than other Americans, and 63 percent of Democrats said the same of Republicans, up from 47 and 35 percent in 2016. [[c-us8-faith-pew2022]] In Congress, Pew's analysis of DW-NOMINATE scores, which place lawmakers by their roll-call votes, found the parties 'farther apart ideologically today than at any time in the past 50 years', with both having 'shifted further away from the center, but Republicans more so.' [[c-us8-faith-congress]] Parties, money and polarization are treated in US2.14.

Pew's 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study, of 36,908 adults, found 62 percent Christian, against 78 percent in 2007 and 71 percent in 2014, and 29 percent unaffiliated, against 16 and 23 percent; since 2019 the Christian share has hovered between 60 and 64 percent. [[c-us8-faith-rls]] In Pew's words the unaffiliated population 'has leveled off – at least temporarily.' [[c-us8-faith-level]] Evangelical Protestants are 23 percent of adults, down from 26 percent in 2007, and mainline Protestants 11 percent, down from 18; Catholics are 19 percent, Jews 2 percent and Muslims 1 percent. [[c-us8-faith-groups]] American Catholics are 36 percent Hispanic. [[c-us8-faith-catholics]] Among validated voters in 2024, 81 percent of white evangelical Protestants and 55 percent of Catholics voted for Trump, while the unaffiliated voted 70 percent for Harris. [[c-us8-faith-vote24]] The rise of the religious right to 1979 is in US7.13, and religion worldwide in 16.9.

Pew estimated about 7.5 million Jewish Americans in 2020, 2.4 percent of adults; 71 percent of Jewish adults were Democrats or leaned Democratic, while 75 percent of Orthodox Jews were Republicans or leaned Republican. [[c-us8-faith-jews]] FBI figures as reported by the ADL counted 1,938 anti-Jewish hate crime incidents in 2024, nearly 70 percent of religion-based hate crimes and the most since the FBI began collecting such data in 1991. [[c-us8-faith-fbi24]] FBI figures as reported by the ADL counted 1,528 anti-Jewish incidents in 2025, 63 percent of 2,408 religion-based incidents, and, as reported by the Algemeiner, 205 against Muslims. The FBI's own summary shows all reported hate-crime incidents falling from 11,679 to 10,881; among agencies that reported at least six common months in both years the fall was 7.0 percent. [[c-us8-faith-fbi25]] The ADL's own audit, which includes non-criminal harassment, counted 6,274 antisemitic incidents in 2025, down a third from 9,354 in 2024, though assaults rose from 196 to 203. [[c-us8-faith-adl]] AP reported that some critics find the ADL's criteria too broad, while Aryeh Tuchman, who formerly led the ADL's Center on Extremism and now directs the Nexus Center for Antisemitism, which AP says 'promotes a more nuanced definition of antisemitism than the ADL uses', said the ADL's approach reflects a genuine concern that anti-Zionism threatens the safety of American Jews. [[c-us8-faith-adl-debate]] For Israel and the Palestinians, see 16.6.

Gallup reported in July 2026 that average confidence in the institutions it tracks was 27 percent, one point above the record low of 2023, with Republicans 13 points more confident than Democrats (36 percent against 23). Small business stood at 67 percent and the military at 61; the police at 45, organized religion at 33, the Supreme Court and the presidency at 27 each, and Congress at 9. [[c-us8-faith-gallup]]

practice.q: The ADL counted 9,354 antisemitic incidents in 2024, while the FBI figures reported by the ADL show 1,938 anti-Jewish hate crime incidents. What best explains the gap?
choices: The ADL counts non-criminal harassment too; the FBI counts hate crimes
The ADL counts just assaults, which the FBI files under other crimes
The FBI recorded more incidents, since the ADL counts each victim just once
The ADL figure covers 2025, the FBI figure an earlier year, 2024
practice.why: The two sources define incidents differently: the audit 'includes both criminal and non-criminal acts', reported to the ADL by victims, law enforcement, the media and partner organizations; the FBI figures count reported hate crimes.

wrong.1: The ADL counts assault, harassment and vandalism; assaults were 196 in 2024 and 203 in 2025.
wrong.2: The FBI figure (1,938) is far below the ADL's (9,354).
wrong.3: Both figures are for 2024; in 2025 the FBI figure reported by the ADL was 1,528 and the ADL's own audit count 6,274.

practice.q: What does Pew's 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study show about the religiously unaffiliated?
choices: Their share rose from 16 to 29 percent and has levelled off for now
Their share has fallen back below 20 percent since its 2014 peak
They now outnumber Christians, who have fallen to 29 percent
Their share is still rising as fast as it did between 2007 and 2014
practice.why: Pew finds 29 percent unaffiliated, up from 16 percent in 2007, and writes that the group 'has leveled off – at least temporarily'.

wrong.1: The share is 29 percent, up from 23 percent in 2014.
wrong.2: Christians are 62 percent of adults; 29 percent is the share of the unaffiliated.
wrong.3: The share rose 7 points in the seven years from 2007 to 2014 but only 6 points in the roughly ten years from 2014 to 2023-24, and Pew says the rise has levelled off, at least temporarily.
